questions.subtopic: Enterprise Governance of Information and Technology (EGIT). Definition
questions.question: A new board asks the IS auditor what enterprise governance of IT (EGIT) covers. Which description is MOST accurate?

options.A: Management processes the CIO uses to plan, build and run enterprise IT
options.B: A regulatory obligation that applies to banks, insurers and other financial firms
options.C: Board-level direction and oversight ensuring IT supports business strategy
options.D: A change-management discipline controlling how releases enter production

questions.key_concept: EGIT is part of enterprise governance: the board directs and oversees IT so it supports strategy, while management executes.
questions.pre_read: Separate governance (direction and accountability) from management (execution) before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 treats EGIT as an integral part of enterprise governance: the board evaluates, directs and monitors so that IT supports strategy and creates value, and accountability stays with the board. Option A describes IT management, which plans, builds, runs and monitors within the direction governance sets. It is necessary, but it is not governance.

wrong_explanations.A: This describes IT management (plan, build, run, monitor). COBIT separates management from governance, which sets direction and holds accountability at board level.
wrong_explanations.B: EGIT applies to every enterprise that depends on IT, not just regulated sectors. Regulation can raise its importance but does not define its scope.
wrong_explanations.D: Change management is one management process. It is far narrower than governance, which directs and oversees all IT-related decisions.

tips: Eliminate: B ties EGIT to regulated sectors, and D shrinks it to a single change process.
Final two: C beats A because governance sets direction with board accountability, while A describes management executing within that direction.
Exam cue: governance means the board evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds, runs and monitors. When scope is asked, pick the board-level answer.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Governance Framework); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); ISO/IEC 38500:2024 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'EGIT definition - integrated enterprise governance with board accountability, IT-business alignment'. Public source: COBIT 2019. All scenario specifics (regional bank, new board briefing) invented for this question. First D2 question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Round 2 review (Oct 2026): framework_ref updated to ISO/IEC 38500:2024.

questions.subtopic: Three Lines Model. Roles and Boundaries
questions.question: An IS auditor briefs the audit committee on the Three Lines Model. Which role assignment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Internal audit owns risk; management oversees it; the board gives assurance
options.B: Risk functions own risk; line managers monitor it; audit approves controls
options.C: Management owns risk; risk functions provide independent assurance; audit advises management
options.D: Management owns risk; risk functions support and challenge; audit independently assures

questions.key_concept: Management owns risk, second-line functions support and challenge, and internal audit alone provides independent assurance to the governing body.
questions.pre_read: Track two things per line: who owns the risk, and who is independent of management.
questions.correct_explanation: In the IIA Three Lines Model, first-line management owns and manages risk, second-line roles such as risk and compliance provide expertise, support, monitoring and challenge, and internal audit gives independent, objective assurance to the governing body. Option C wrongly makes the second line independent; it supports management, so only internal audit is independent.

wrong_explanations.A: This inverts the model. Audit cannot own risk without losing independence, and the board is the governing body that receives assurance.
wrong_explanations.B: Operational management, not risk functions, owns risk. Audit evaluates controls; approving them would create a self-review threat.
wrong_explanations.C: Second-line functions sit within management and support it. They monitor and challenge but are not independent; independent assurance is the third line's role.

tips: Eliminate: A has audit owning risk, and B moves risk ownership away from operational management.
Final two: D beats C because only internal audit is independent of management; the second line supports and challenges but is not independent.
Exam cue: in role questions, find the owner (management) and the only independent assurer (internal audit), then check nobody else claims independence.
questions.framework_ref: IIA Three Lines Model (2020); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 7.1 (Organizational Independence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Three Lines Model - three distinct accountabilities (own / support / independently assure), distinct from inverted-roles / audit-owns-all / COSO-conflation'. Public source: IIA Three Lines Model (2020). All scenario specifics (health-insurance company, audit committee briefing) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Steering Committee. Composition and Responsibility
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the charter of a manufacturer's IT steering committee. Which design feature is MOST important?

options.A: Senior business and IT leaders jointly prioritizing IT investments
options.B: IT leaders alone deciding priorities based on technical expertise
options.C: External consultants chairing meetings to keep decisions independent
options.D: Business-unit heads alone setting IT priorities for the enterprise

questions.key_concept: An IT steering committee aligns IT with business strategy through joint senior business and IT decisions on priorities and investments.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee is for, alignment, then which composition can actually deliver it.
questions.correct_explanation: An IT steering committee exists to align IT with the business, so it needs senior business and IT leaders deciding together on investment priorities, with executive sponsorship. Option D keeps the business in charge but drops IT's view of feasibility, risk and capacity, so priorities can be set that IT cannot deliver safely. Alignment is a two-way discussion.

wrong_explanations.B: An IT-only committee filters business priorities through technical preference, which is the misalignment the committee is meant to prevent.
wrong_explanations.C: Consultants can advise, but decision authority and accountability for IT priorities must stay with the enterprise's own leaders.
wrong_explanations.D: Business-only priority setting ignores IT feasibility, capacity and risk, so alignment fails in the other direction.

tips: Eliminate: B lets IT set priorities without the business, and C hands decisions to outsiders who carry no accountability.
Final two: A beats D because alignment needs business demand and IT capability weighed together; a business-only committee still misaligns.
Exam cue: for steering committees, pick cross-functional senior membership with decision authority over IT priorities.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT Steering Committee - cross-functional composition with executive sponsorship, responsible for strategy/investment/alignment, distinct from IT-only / business-only / external-consultant-run'. Public source: COBIT 2019 + ISACA EGIT. All scenario specifics (mid-size discrete-parts manufacturer) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Strategy. Alignment with Business Strategy
questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing whether a retailer's three-year IT strategy is aligned with the business. Which evidence is MOST convincing?

options.A: The CIO set the strategy and shared it for information
options.B: Every major investment traces to a measurable business objective
options.C: The roadmap adopts the newest technologies available in the sector
options.D: Business-unit heads formally signed off the final strategy document

questions.key_concept: IT-business alignment is evidenced by tracing each major IT investment to a business objective with a measure of success.
questions.pre_read: Distinguish evidence that people agreed from evidence that investments actually serve business goals.
questions.correct_explanation: Alignment is shown by traceability: every major IT investment should map to a business objective with a measure, so gaps in either direction become visible and progress can be judged. Option D shows the business agreed to the document, but sign-off does not prove investments serve objectives; leaders often approve plans they have not tested against strategy.

wrong_explanations.A: A CIO-only strategy shared for information shows IT acting alone. Alignment requires business input and approval, not notification.
wrong_explanations.C: Adopting the newest technology reflects ambition, not alignment. Investments must be justified by business objectives, whatever their novelty.
wrong_explanations.D: Formal sign-off shows agreement with the document, but it does not prove each investment supports a business objective or that success can be measured.

tips: Eliminate: A has the CIO acting without business approval, and C chases technology for its own sake.
Final two: B beats D because traceability to measurable objectives proves alignment, while sign-off only proves agreement.
Exam cue: when asked for the BEST evidence of alignment, choose the mapping of IT investments to business objectives over approvals or opinions.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 (Goals Cascade and Performance Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT strategy alignment - explicit mapping of IT investments to business objectives with measurable success criteria, distinct from technical-ambition / identical-strategies / CIO-only-authoring'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO02. All scenario specifics (retail e-commerce, 3-year IT strategy) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company runs governance, risk and compliance as three separate functions with duplicated assessments. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Merge the three functions into one GRC department under one executive
options.B: Keep the three functions separate, each with its own tools and data
options.C: Move the three responsibilities into internal audit to avoid duplication
options.D: Keep distinct functions but share a risk taxonomy, platform and reporting

questions.key_concept: Integrated GRC keeps distinct functions and accountabilities but shares taxonomy, technology and reporting to remove duplication and gaps.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the problem is structure or coordination before choosing a fix.
questions.correct_explanation: Integrated GRC keeps the specialist roles and authorities of governance, risk and compliance but connects how they work: a shared risk taxonomy, a common platform and coordinated reporting remove duplicated assessments and gaps. Option A also removes duplication, but merging blurs distinct accountabilities and expertise; integration is about shared processes and data, not one organizational box.

wrong_explanations.A: A merger may cut cost, but it blurs distinct accountabilities and specialist expertise. Integration needs shared processes and data, not a single department.
wrong_explanations.B: Full separation keeps the duplication and inconsistent terminology that caused the problem, and leaves gaps between functions unmanaged.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit must stay independent. Taking ownership of governance, risk and compliance would make it audit its own work.

tips: Eliminate: B preserves the duplication, and C puts audit in a management role it would later audit.
Final two: D beats A because integration connects processes and data while keeping clear accountabilities; a merger blurs who owns what.
Exam cue: for GRC, prefer coordinated processes, a shared taxonomy and common platforms over structural mergers.
questions.framework_ref: OCEG GRC Capability Model; COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance with External Requirements); IIA Three Lines Model (2020)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'GRC integration - functional separation maintained while integrating processes/technology/data, distinct from full-merger / full-independence / consolidation-under-audit'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + OCEG GRC. All scenario specifics (global pharma, three independent GRC departments) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A SaaS company's board has delegated all information security matters to the CISO. Which statement BEST describes the board's accountability?

options.A: It transfers to the CISO with the delegated authority
options.B: It sits with the CFO, who controls the security budget
options.C: It remains with the board, even though execution is delegated
options.D: It lapses, since security is a management matter

questions.key_concept: The board keeps accountability for information security governance; it delegates execution to the CISO, not ultimate responsibility.
questions.pre_read: Separate who does the work from who answers for the outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Boards can delegate execution of information security to the CISO and management, but they cannot delegate accountability. The board still sets direction, approves risk appetite, checks resources and oversees major incidents; NIST CSF 2.0 added the Govern function to make this explicit. Option A confuses delegation of authority with transfer of accountability, which stays with the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Delegation passes authority to act, not accountability. The board must still oversee security strategy, risk appetite and performance.
wrong_explanations.B: Funding is one input. Accountability for security governance sits with the board as a whole, not the executive who manages the budget.
wrong_explanations.D: Security risk is a business risk the board must oversee. Calling it a management matter confuses who executes with who is accountable, and accountability never lapses.

tips: Eliminate: B pins accountability on the budget holder, and D treats security as purely a management matter.
Final two: C beats A because accountability cannot be delegated; only execution moves to the CISO.
Exam cue: when a stem says the board delegated something, remember authority can move down but accountability stays at the top.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27014 (Governance of Information Security); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF) v2.0 (February 2024)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'board accountability for information-security governance - non-delegable, execution delegates to CISO, accountability stays at board level'. Public source: NIST CSF v2.0 + ISACA InfoSec Governance. All scenario specifics (B2B SaaS platform, board delegating all to CISO) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Risk Management Lifecycle. Identify / Assess / Respond / Monitor
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews an IT risk management program. Which finding indicates the MOST significant gap in the risk lifecycle?

options.A: Most registered risks lack a documented response or monitoring
options.B: Risk identification last ran 18 months ago, not every year
options.C: Risks are rated on a qualitative heat map, not in dollars
options.D: The board receives a summary of risks once a year

questions.key_concept: Risk management adds value only when identified risks are treated and monitored; a register without responses gives false assurance.
questions.pre_read: Walk the lifecycle (identify, assess, respond, monitor) and ask where exposure is left unmanaged.
questions.correct_explanation: The lifecycle only reduces exposure when identified risks receive a response and are monitored. If most registered risks have neither, the program has catalogued exposure without managing it, and the register gives false comfort. Option B is a real weakness, but late identification only delays the cycle, whereas in option A risks already known are left untreated.

wrong_explanations.B: A delayed identification cycle is a timeliness gap, but known risks can still be treated. Unanswered, unmonitored risks are the larger failure.
wrong_explanations.C: Qualitative heat maps are an accepted assessment method when data is limited. Using them is not a lifecycle gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Annual board reporting may be thin, but it is a reporting cadence choice. The core failure lies in risks that receive no response.

tips: Eliminate: C uses an accepted qualitative method, and D is a reporting cadence that can be tuned.
Final two: A beats B because identified risks left untreated are unmanaged exposure now, while late identification only slows the cycle.
Exam cue: in lifecycle questions, a broken respond-and-monitor stage outranks weaknesses in how risks are found or rated.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk-management lifecycle - response and monitor stages broken when 86% of identified risks have no response, more significant than identification timing or assessment method'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ISO 31000. All scenario specifics (regional telecom, 140 risks, top-20 only responded/monitored, annual board reporting) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Separation of Duties Within IT. Practical SoD Design
questions.question: At a small bank, an IS auditor reviews IT role assignments. Which combination is the GREATEST segregation-of-duties concern?

options.A: Developers deploying their own code through a version-controlled pipeline
options.B: One manager holding database, system administrator and code-change rights
options.C: Help-desk staff who can view, but not change, production data
options.D: A security analyst reviewing logs without rights to alter them

questions.key_concept: Segregation of duties fails most when one person can change data or code and also alter the logs that would detect it.
questions.pre_read: For each role, ask: can this person make a change and also hide it?
questions.correct_explanation: The manager can change data, alter production code and, as system administrator, modify the logs that would reveal it. That toxic combination lets one person commit and conceal an error or fraud. Option A is a real segregation weakness, but version-controlled changes leave an audit trail; the manager's combined rights can erase that trail.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-deployment removes a second review and needs fixing, but the code changes remain recorded in version control and can be detected.
wrong_explanations.C: Viewing rights without change rights for help-desk staff are appropriately restricted and create no segregation-of-duties conflict.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing logs without the ability to change them is good segregation. It supports detection rather than weakening it.

tips: Eliminate: C and D describe properly restricted roles with no conflicting rights.
Final two: B beats A because one person who can change data, code and logs can also hide the change; A's changes stay traceable.
Exam cue: the worst segregation conflict is the one that lets a person both act and erase the evidence.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SoD within IT toxic combination analysis - DBA + system admin + code modification in one person on core-banking system as most severe, distinct from developer-self-deployment / physical-plus-logical-access / read-only'. Public source: ISACA IT Audit Standards + COBIT 2019. All scenario specifics (community bank, 8 IT staff, four observation patterns) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): spelled out DBA.

questions.subtopic: Audit's Role in EGIT. Independent Evaluation of Governance
questions.question: During an EGIT audit, the CEO asks the IS audit director to also advise the IT steering committee and join it permanently. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Accept both roles, since audit expertise strengthens governance decisions
options.B: Join the governance committee permanently but decline advice during the audit
options.C: Withdraw from the audit and refer it to an outside specialist
options.D: Continue the audit while declining both of the requested roles

questions.key_concept: Internal audit evaluates EGIT independently; advisory or decision-making roles in the governance it audits create self-review threats.
questions.pre_read: For each requested role, ask whether audit would later evaluate its own work.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal audit's role in EGIT is independent evaluation. Advising on governance design during the engagement and sitting permanently on the committee would both have the auditor later assessing decisions they helped make, a self-review threat. Option B avoids the immediate conflict but keeps the ongoing one: permanent membership makes audit part of the governance it must assess.

wrong_explanations.A: Both roles create self-review threats. Expertise does not outweigh the need for audit to stay independent of the decisions it evaluates.
wrong_explanations.B: Declining mid-audit advice removes one threat, but permanent membership makes audit part of the governance it must later evaluate.
wrong_explanations.C: Independent evaluation of EGIT is audit's proper role. Abandoning it is an overreaction; only the conflicting roles need to be declined.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts both conflicting roles, and C abandons the legitimate audit role.
Final two: D beats B because permanent committee membership is an ongoing self-review threat, not just a mid-engagement one.
Exam cue: audit can evaluate governance or help run it, never both; decline any role that makes audit part of what it assures.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1002 (Organizational Independence); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 2.2 (Safeguarding Objectivity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit role in EGIT - independent evaluation only, decline mid-engagement advisory (immediate self-review) and permanent committee membership (ongoing self-review), offer alternatives'. Public source: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics + IIA Three Lines + Standard 1003. All scenario specifics (publicly-traded insurer, CEO requesting three concurrent roles) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Round 2 review (Oct 2026): key reworded as one clause to remove the two-part tell.

questions.subtopic: Auditing IT Governance Structure and Implementation
questions.question: An IS audit manager finds the IT governance charter's meeting, approval, board-review and annual-update requirements have all been missed for years. Which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: The charter is well designed; the lapses are routine operational issues
options.B: Each lapse is a separate operational issue to report to its owner
options.C: Governance exists on paper, not in practice, and cannot self-correct
options.D: The charter should be discarded and a new framework adopted

questions.key_concept: Auditing IT governance tests design and practice; consistent divergence, including a lapsed review cycle, is itself a systemic finding.
questions.pre_read: Look for what the separate observations have in common before choosing a conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: Seen together, the lapses show documented governance and actual practice have diverged on every requirement, including the charter's own update cycle. That pattern is the finding: governance exists on paper only, and the mechanism that should have caught the drift has also failed. Option B reports symptoms one by one and misses the common root cause the board needs to see.

wrong_explanations.A: Auditing governance covers design and implementation. A charter nobody follows provides no governance, whatever its design quality.
wrong_explanations.B: Separate reports treat symptoms and hide the shared root cause: governance discipline has broken down, including the charter's own review cycle.
wrong_explanations.D: Replacing the framework does not fix weak discipline; a new charter would drift the same way unless the root cause is addressed.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores implementation entirely, and D replaces the document instead of fixing the discipline.
Final two: C beats B because the pattern across every requirement is the root-cause finding; reporting each lapse separately hides it.
Exam cue: when several lapses share one cause, report the systemic finding to governance rather than isolated items to owners.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); ISO/IEC 38500:2024 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'auditing IT governance structure - synthesis finding when documented governance and operational practice diverge across multiple dimensions AND self-correction mechanism is also broken'. questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a CRO's draft IT risk management program. Which element is MOST essential?

options.A: A risk charter assigning ownership, appetite and accountability
options.B: A complete risk register with likelihood and impact ratings
options.C: A catalog of preventive and detective controls across IT
options.D: Cyber insurance transferring the financial impact of IT losses

questions.key_concept: An IT risk program rests on governance: defined appetite, ownership and accountability that drive identification, assessment, response and monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Ask which element the other components depend on to produce decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: A defensible program starts with governance: a charter that sets risk appetite and names who owns, decides and reports on each risk. Identification, assessment, response and monitoring all depend on that structure. Option B is a necessary component, but a register with no owners or appetite cannot drive decisions; risks are listed and nobody is accountable for treating them.

wrong_explanations.B: A register is needed, but without ownership and appetite nobody decides on responses, so listed risks go untreated.
wrong_explanations.C: Controls selected without identified and assessed risks may protect the wrong things. Controls are a response, not the program's foundation.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance transfers only financial impact and is one treatment option. It cannot replace identifying, owning and monitoring IT risks.

tips: Eliminate: C deploys controls with no risk basis, and D relies on one treatment option, transfer.
Final two: A beats B because governance assigns the ownership and appetite that make a register usable; a register alone has no decision-maker.
Exam cue: when asked what a program needs MOST, choose the governance element (ownership, appetite, accountability) before any operational component.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT risk-management program components - five integrated elements (governance + identification + assessment + response + monitoring), distinct from identification-only / controls-only / insurance-only'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ISO 31000. All scenario specifics (mid-cap energy company, CRO draft program) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Risk Analysis Methods. Qualitative vs Quantitative Selection
questions.question: A CIO wants dollar-based quantitative analysis for every IT risk, though loss data is sparse for many. What should the IS auditor advise as MOST important?

options.A: Apply one method to all risks so results stay comparable
options.B: Match the method to available data and the decision's purpose
options.C: Use quantitative analysis everywhere, because dollar values are objective
options.D: Use qualitative ratings everywhere, because they are faster to produce

questions.key_concept: Choose qualitative, semi-quantitative or quantitative risk analysis based on available data and the decision it must support.
questions.pre_read: Notice that loss data is sparse; it decides how credible quantitative output would be.
questions.correct_explanation: Method choice should follow the data available and what the decision needs. Quantitative analysis is credible only where loss data supports the estimates; with sparse data it produces precise-looking but unreliable numbers. Qualitative or semi-quantitative methods fit those risks. Option A values comparability, but forcing one method onto risks it does not fit undermines the results being compared.

wrong_explanations.A: Consistency aids comparison, but applying an ill-fitting method everywhere produces unreliable results. Fitness for purpose comes first.
wrong_explanations.C: Without sufficient loss data, dollar figures rest on guesses and give false precision. Quantitative output is only as objective as its inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Speed is not the criterion. Where good data exists and decisions need financial values, quantitative analysis adds real value.

tips: Eliminate: C and D each force one method on every risk regardless of the data behind it.
Final two: B beats A because fitness for purpose decides the method; consistency is no help if the method does not suit the data.
Exam cue: when data is sparse, prefer judgment-based or semi-quantitative analysis; precise numbers built on guesses mislead decision-makers.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); IEC 31010:2019 (Risk Assessment Techniques); FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk-analysis method selection - data + objective, semi-quantitative as middle ground, distinct from universal-quantitative / universal-qualitative / consistency-over-fit'. questions.subtopic: Data Privacy Program Design. Core Elements
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a genomics company's privacy program under GDPR and HIPAA. Which element is the MOST essential foundation?

options.A: A detailed privacy notice published on the company's public website
options.B: A named privacy officer with an inventory of personal data
options.C: Strong encryption and need-to-know access for genetic records
options.D: One policy document covering every applicable privacy regulation

questions.key_concept: A privacy program starts with accountable governance and an inventory of personal data, purposes and lawful bases; security controls support it.
questions.pre_read: Separate protecting data (security) from using it lawfully and fairly (privacy).
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy compliance depends on knowing what personal data is held, why and on what lawful basis, and on someone accountable for decisions about it. Rights handling, breach response, vendor terms and training all build on that. Option C protects confidentiality, which is necessary, but security controls cannot show lawful processing, purpose limitation or respect for data-subject rights.

wrong_explanations.A: A notice informs data subjects but creates no accountability, inventory or process for rights and breaches behind it.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption and access control protect confidentiality, but privacy also requires lawful basis, purpose limits and rights handling, which security alone cannot provide.
wrong_explanations.D: A policy states intent. Without accountable owners, a data inventory and operating processes, it does not show the regulations are met.

tips: Eliminate: A and D are documents that state intent without any operating mechanism.
Final two: B beats C because privacy is governed through accountability and knowing your data; encryption protects data but cannot prove lawful use.
Exam cue: privacy is wider than security; look for accountability and a data inventory before technical safeguards.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Articles 5 and 24 (EU Regulation 2016/679); GDPR Article 30 (Records of Processing Activities); HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart E); GINA (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act); ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (Privacy Information Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'data privacy program design - 8 integrated elements (governance, inventory, lawful basis, rights, breach, vendors, training, monitoring), distinct from notice-only / encryption-only / policy-only'. Public source: GDPR + HIPAA + GINA + ISACA Privacy. All scenario specifics (consumer-genomics company, multi-regulation context) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: After a merger, a firm runs three overlapping CRM systems, and each IT team argues for its own. Which basis should the IS auditor recommend as BEST for choosing one?

options.A: The platform with the lowest current annual running cost
options.B: The platform supported by the largest internal IT team
options.C: The platform used by the acquiring company before the merger
options.D: Required business capabilities mapped against each platform

questions.key_concept: EA rationalizes overlapping systems by mapping required business capabilities to each platform, with cost as one input.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the merged business needs the system to do before comparing platforms.
questions.correct_explanation: Enterprise architecture rationalizes overlapping systems by starting from the business capabilities the merged firm needs, then assessing how well each platform supports them, along with cost, risk and integration. Lowest running cost is a fair input, but choosing on cost alone can keep a cheap system that cannot support key processes, pushing larger costs into workarounds and later replacement.

wrong_explanations.A: Running cost is one input, not the deciding basis. A cheap platform that misses needed capabilities creates larger costs later.
wrong_explanations.B: Team size reflects IT history, not business need. Choosing on internal support numbers lets IT preference override capability fit.
wrong_explanations.C: The acquirer's system is not automatically the best fit. Defaulting to it is a political choice, not an architecture decision.

tips: Eliminate: B and C decide by IT history or deal politics rather than business need.
Final two: D beats A because capability fit drives the choice and cost is one input; lowest cost alone can buy a poor fit.
Exam cue: in architecture rationalization, start from business capabilities, then weigh cost, risk and integration.
questions.framework_ref: TOGAF Standard; COBIT 2019 APO03 (Managed Enterprise Architecture); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'cloud governance Shared Responsibility Model - service-model-dependent split with provider and customer responsibilities, distinct from provider-everything / customer-everything / universal-boundary'. questions.subtopic: KPIs vs KRIs vs KCIs. Distinction
questions.question: Management at a logistics firm uses KPIs, KRIs and KCIs interchangeably. Which distinction should the IS auditor recommend as MOST accurate?

options.A: KPIs track goal achievement, KRIs track risk exposure, KCIs track control operation
options.B: KPIs give leading signals, KRIs give lagging signals, KCIs show real-time status
options.C: KPIs track financial results, KRIs track operations, KCIs track compliance
options.D: KPIs, KRIs and KCIs are alternative labels for one measure

questions.key_concept: KPIs measure goal achievement, KRIs measure risk exposure and its trend, and KCIs measure whether controls operate effectively.
questions.pre_read: For each indicator, ask what question it answers, not when it is measured.
questions.correct_explanation: Each indicator answers a different question. KPIs show how well objectives are being achieved, KRIs signal the level or movement of risk exposure, and KCIs show whether specific controls are operating as intended. Option B classifies by timing, but any of the three can be leading or lagging; timing does not define the type, and KRIs are usually forward-looking.

wrong_explanations.B: Timing is not the distinction. KRIs are usually designed as early warnings, and KPIs and KCIs can be leading or lagging.
wrong_explanations.C: Indicators are not split by business area. Each type can measure financial, operational or compliance matters.
wrong_explanations.D: The three measure different things for different decisions. Treating them as one hides rising risk behind good performance figures.

tips: Eliminate: C splits indicators by business area, and D treats them as one measure.
Final two: A beats B because indicator type is set by what is measured, not by timing; KRIs are usually forward-looking.
Exam cue: performance asks whether goals are met, risk asks whether exposure is rising, control asks whether the control works.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 MEA01 (Managed Performance and Conformance Monitoring); COBIT 2019 MEA02 (Managed System of Internal Control); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'KPI vs KRI vs KCI distinction - by what each measures (objective achievement / risk exposure / control effectiveness), not by category / timing / interchangeable'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + COBIT 2019. All scenario specifics (freight-logistics company, inconsistent application) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): options rewritten as full statements.

questions.question: A bank holds regulated customer data, employee records and public material. Which feature of its classification scheme should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Labeling every dataset Restricted so nothing is under-protected
options.B: Custom protection rules tailored to each individual data record
options.C: A few levels, each tied to defined handling requirements
options.D: Many levels aligned to each regulation's own data categories

questions.key_concept: Effective classification uses a few levels, each tied to handling requirements, with regulatory obligations mapped onto those levels.
questions.pre_read: Judge each scheme by whether staff could apply it consistently every day.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification works when a small number of levels each carry clear handling rules for storage, access, transmission and retention, so staff and tools can apply them consistently. Regulatory requirements are mapped onto those levels. Option D looks precise, but many levels confuse users and cause inconsistent labeling; regulations should map to a few levels, not define their own.

wrong_explanations.A: Over-classifying everything raises cost, blocks legitimate use and trains staff to ignore labels, so truly sensitive data loses distinction.
wrong_explanations.B: Record-by-record rules cannot be applied or enforced consistently at scale. Classification works by data type and level.
wrong_explanations.D: Aligning levels to every regulation multiplies them; extra levels look precise but confuse users and tools, causing inconsistent labeling. Regulatory needs are better mapped onto a few levels.

tips: Eliminate: A over-protects everything, and B cannot be applied consistently at scale.
Final two: C beats D because a few levels with clear handling rules are applied reliably; many levels create confusion and mislabeling.
Exam cue: a classification scheme is only as good as its handling rules and how consistently people apply them.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems); NIST SP 800-60 (Data Categorization); GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'data classification - small number of levels tied to handling requirements, classified by type with automated tooling, distinct from over-classify / per-record / judgment-only'. Public source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 + NIST SP 800-60 + ISACA. All scenario specifics (national bank, GLBA + state PII + marketing + operational) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Management proposes moving the help desk to an offshore provider for a 21% cost saving. Which response by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Approve it: the saving is material and contract terms can absorb risks
options.B: Stay out of it, since sourcing is management's strategic decision
options.C: Draft contract clauses for data residency and knowledge transfer
options.D: Ensure the decision weighs data residency, knowledge loss and flexibility

questions.key_concept: In outsourcing decisions, the auditor ensures management weighs all material risks beyond cost, without taking the decision itself.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the decision and what the auditor must make sure they see.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor adds value by making sure the decision-maker sees every material factor beyond the 21% saving: loss of institutional knowledge, data-residency exposure from offshore processing, reduced oversight and lost flexibility. Management then decides. Option C addresses real risks, but drafting contract terms puts the auditor in a management role and still covers only some of the factors.

wrong_explanations.A: A material saving does not settle the decision. Contracts cannot fully offset knowledge loss, data-residency exposure or lost flexibility.
wrong_explanations.B: The decision is management's, but outsourcing changes the risk profile. Giving objective risk input preserves independence, provided management still decides.
wrong_explanations.C: Designing contract controls is management's job and could impair independence. It also skips the prior question of whether the move is sound.

tips: Eliminate: A decides on cost alone, and B withholds the risk input audit is expected to give.
Final two: D beats C because the auditor ensures risks are weighed by decision-makers; drafting contract terms is a management task.
Exam cue: on sourcing decisions, the auditor informs the decision with risks beyond cost and leaves the choice to management.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'outsourcing decision - auditor surfaces multi-factor analysis (cost + knowledge + data residency + reporting line + contract flexibility) for decision-maker, distinct from cost-only-recommend / knowledge-only-veto / full-recusal'. Public source: ITAF + IIA Practice Guide. All scenario specifics (mid-size manufacturer, IT help-desk outsourcing, five specific facts) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): explanation no longer cites a contract minimum absent from the stem.

questions.subtopic: IT HR Management. Mandatory Vacation + Succession in Fraud-Risk Roles
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews HR controls for IT staff. Which observation indicates the GREATEST fraud risk?

options.A: A retiring network engineer with unique knowledge and no successor
options.B: Help-desk staff without formal succession but with fully documented work
options.C: A financial-database DBA who never takes leave and refuses cross-training
options.D: Security staff rotated through shifts with enforced annual leave

questions.key_concept: Mandatory leave and cross-training expose concealed fraud; a privileged user who avoids both is a high fraud-risk signal.
questions.pre_read: Separate risks of losing knowledge from risks of someone hiding what they do.
questions.correct_explanation: A person who manipulates records usually has to stay in control of them to keep the scheme hidden. Someone with financial-database rights who avoids leave and resists cross-training shows exactly that pattern, and nobody else ever looks at the work. Option A is a serious continuity risk, but it concerns losing knowledge, not concealing fraud.

wrong_explanations.A: Missing succession creates continuity and operational risk. It does not suggest someone is concealing manipulation, so it ranks lower on fraud risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Documented work that any staff member can perform limits both continuity and fraud risk. Formal succession would be a minor improvement.
wrong_explanations.D: Rotation and enforced leave are fraud-deterrent controls. They expose any concealed activity to other staff.

tips: Eliminate: B has documented, shared work, and D shows rotation and enforced leave working as intended.
Final two: C beats A because avoiding leave and cross-training protects a concealed scheme; A is a continuity risk, not a fraud signal.
Exam cue: sensitive access combined with no leave and no backup is the classic fraud red flag; mandatory vacation exists to expose it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); COBIT 2019 APO07 (Managed Human Resources); ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT HR fraud-risk pattern - DBA with no extended vacation + refusal to cross-train + financial-system access as textbook scheme-protection, distinct from succession-only / role-rotation-as-weakness / help-desk-succession'. Public source: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual + ISACA Fraud Risk Management. All scenario specifics (agricultural cooperative, four IT HR observations) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Enterprise Change Management. Failed Acquisition Integration
questions.question: Eighteen months after an acquisition, IT integration is late and over budget, yet the program board still reports it 'on track'. Which finding should the IS auditor rate MOST significant?

options.A: The budget overrun, now well past plan, with no agreed completion date
options.B: Governance reporting that contradicts the program's actual status
options.C: Normal post-acquisition delay that will resolve over time
options.D: A need to unwind the acquisition and write off spend

questions.key_concept: In enterprise change, inaccurate status reporting to governance is the most severe failure because it disables course correction.
questions.pre_read: Ask which problem stops the organization from fixing all the others.
questions.correct_explanation: Schedule slippage and cost overrun are real, but they are symptoms that governance could correct. When the program board reports 'on track' against contrary metrics, the people who could intervene are misinformed, so every other problem continues unchecked. Option A is serious, yet tighter cost control cannot work while governance is told nothing is wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: The overrun is a serious symptom, but fixing cost control does not help while governance believes the program is on track and does not intervene.
wrong_explanations.C: Late, over-budget delivery with misreported status is not normal friction. Treating it as routine leaves the root problem unaddressed.
wrong_explanations.D: Unwinding is a business decision beyond the audit finding, and it skips correcting the governance reporting that allowed the drift.

tips: Eliminate: C dismisses clear warning signs, and D jumps to a drastic business decision outside audit's role.
Final two: B beats A because misreporting stops governance from correcting anything, including the cost overrun.
Exam cue: when status reports contradict the metrics, the reporting failure outranks the problems it hides.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI05 (Managed Organizational Change); COBIT 2019 BAI01 (Managed Programs); COBIT 2019 MEA01 (Managed Performance and Conformance Monitoring)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'enterprise change management multi-dimensional failure - schedule + people + due-diligence + cost + governance-reporting disconnect, with reporting disconnect as most severe single finding because it disables correction'. Public source: COBIT 2019 BAI05 + ISACA ECM. All scenario specifics (retail-pharmacy chain, 18-month post-acquisition status, five specific facts) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): change board renamed program board.

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance. IT QA Program Effectiveness
questions.question: After a 30% QA budget cut, pre-release defect fixes stay high but production defects rise 40%; the CIO tells the board QA is effective. Which conclusion is BEST for the IS auditor?

options.A: QA is deteriorating, and its reporting to the board is misleading
options.B: QA is effective, as pre-release remediation remains high
options.C: Restoring the QA budget will return the function to its prior performance
options.D: QA has failed and should be replaced by a new function

questions.key_concept: QA effectiveness is judged by outcomes and accurate governance reporting, not by a single favorable internal metric.
questions.pre_read: Compare what QA measures before release with what users experience after it.
questions.correct_explanation: The favorable pre-release figure hides a capacity loss that now shows up as more production defects. Telling the board QA is effective is misleading, so governance cannot react. Option C targets the capacity cause, but it ignores the reporting failure; without accurate reporting the board cannot judge whether restored funding is enough or working.

wrong_explanations.B: Pre-release remediation measures only defects QA found. Rising production defects show more are now being missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Capacity is one cause, but this answer ignores the misleading board reporting. Funding alone does not restore governance's ability to see the trend.
wrong_explanations.D: The program still catches many defects. Calling it a total failure overreacts; capacity and reporting need fixing, not replacement.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts one favorable metric, and D overreacts to a fixable decline.
Final two: A beats C because it captures both the decline and the misleading board reporting; C fixes funding but leaves governance uninformed.
Exam cue: when an internal metric looks good but outcomes worsen, trust the outcomes and check what governance is being told.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality); COBIT 2019 MEA01 (Managed Performance and Conformance Monitoring); ISO 9001:2015
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT QA program effectiveness evaluation - capacity + leading indicators + reporting accuracy, distinct from favorable-metric-only / total-failure / single-dimension fixes'. Public source: ITAF QA + COBIT 2019 BAI03. All scenario specifics (aerospace contractor, four QA program observations) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Risk Register. Definition and Purpose
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how management uses its IT risk register. Which use reflects its PRIMARY purpose?

options.A: Logging remediation actions completed during the fiscal year
options.B: Recording each identified IT risk's likelihood and impact ratings for reference
options.C: Prioritizing, assigning owners and tracking responses to IT risks
options.D: Providing an annual regulatory filing attested by the CRO

questions.key_concept: An IT risk register supports prioritization, owned response decisions and monitoring across the risk lifecycle, not just storage of ratings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decision each register entry should help someone make.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk register is the working tool of the risk program: each entry records the risk, its rating, controls, residual risk, owner and response status, so management can prioritize, decide and monitor. Option B describes part of its content, but a register used only to store ratings supports no decisions; ownership and response tracking make it useful.

wrong_explanations.A: A remediation log records past actions. The register covers current risks, their owners and pending responses, not just completed fixes.
wrong_explanations.B: Ratings are part of each entry, but recording them alone does not drive decisions. Owners and response status turn the list into a management tool.
wrong_explanations.D: Some regulators review registers, but the register is a management tool for running the risk program, not a filing.

tips: Eliminate: A is a remediation log, and D treats a management tool as a regulatory filing.
Final two: C beats B because the register exists to drive owned decisions and follow-up; ratings alone are a static list.
Exam cue: a risk register without owners and response status is a list, not risk management.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT risk register foundational definition - structured catalog with 6 attributes supporting lifecycle decisions, distinct from remediation log / audit-only / regulatory filing'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ISO 31000. Foundational tier launches in D2 batch 3 (mirrors D1 pattern: foundational at D1 batch 6). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Risk Treatment Options. Accept / Reduce / Transfer / Avoid
questions.question: A planned analytics project's privacy risk far exceeds appetite, and no available control or insurance brings it within appetite. Which treatment should management choose as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Accept the risk with senior management sign-off
options.B: Reduce the risk with additional monitoring controls
options.C: Transfer the risk to the analytics vendor by contract
options.D: Avoid the risk by redesigning or canceling the initiative

questions.key_concept: The four treatments are accept, reduce, transfer and avoid; when no other treatment brings a risk within appetite, avoid it.
questions.pre_read: Note that the risk exceeds appetite and cannot be reduced. Ask which treatment remains.
questions.correct_explanation: When a risk far exceeds appetite and no control or insurance can bring it within limits, management should avoid it by redesigning or dropping the activity that creates it. Acceptance is the tempting runner-up because senior sign-off looks like governance, but accepting a risk far beyond board-set appetite overrides that appetite rather than respecting it.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting risk far beyond appetite needs exceptional board-level approval. While the project is only planned and can be redesigned or dropped, sign-off would override the appetite needlessly.
wrong_explanations.B: The stem states no available control brings the risk within appetite, so more monitoring would detect harm without reducing exposure enough.
wrong_explanations.C: A controller stays accountable for personal data its vendors process. A contract can shift costs but cannot transfer the privacy risk or accountability.

tips: Eliminate: B adds controls the stem says cannot work, and C tries to contract away privacy accountability that stays with the controller.
Final two: D beats A because the project is still only planned; accepting risk far beyond appetite would override the board's limits when avoidance is available.
Exam cue: when no control or transfer brings a new, planned activity within appetite, avoid it; acceptance suits risk within appetite or rare board-approved exceptions.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk treatment options foundational - the four standard responses (accept/reduce/transfer/avoid), distinct from incident response (detect/respond/document/report) and lifecycle stages (identify/assess/respond/monitor)'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ISO 31000. Distinct from D1 d1_033 (which covered the same options at application tier with a scenario). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. v2: retargeted to an applied accept-versus-avoid decision to avoid duplicating d2_070. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): aligned acceptance rule with other items: above-appetite acceptance is a rare board-approved exception.

questions.subtopic: Strategic Planning vs Tactical Planning in IT
questions.question: An IT steering committee is reviewing its planning documents. Which statement BEST distinguishes the strategic plan from the tactical plan?

options.A: Strategic sets multi-year direction; tactical turns it into annual initiatives
options.B: Strategic is written by IT; tactical is written by the business
options.C: Strategic sets the IT budget; tactical sets IT staffing levels
options.D: Strategic covers enterprise-wide IT; tactical covers each business unit

questions.key_concept: Strategic IT plans set multi-year direction aligned to enterprise strategy; tactical plans turn that direction into near-term initiatives.
questions.pre_read: Look for time horizon and level of detail as the dividing line.
questions.correct_explanation: Strategic planning sets long-term direction, usually three to five years, and allocates IT resources in line with enterprise strategy. Tactical planning translates that direction into shorter-term initiatives, projects and operational decisions. Option D confuses horizon with scope; both plans can cover the whole enterprise, and business-unit plans still need both a strategic and a tactical layer.

wrong_explanations.B: Both plans need business and IT input. Splitting authorship between them breaks the alignment that planning is meant to deliver.
wrong_explanations.C: Budget and staffing appear at both levels. The distinction is time horizon and level of detail, not which input each controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Scope is not the difference. An enterprise-wide plan can be tactical, and a unit plan can have strategic and tactical layers.

tips: Eliminate: B splits authorship between IT and the business, and C reduces each plan to one input.
Final two: A beats D because the distinction is time horizon and level of detail, not organizational scope.
Exam cue: strategic answers where IT is going over several years; tactical answers what it will do this year to get there.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'strategic vs tactical IT planning foundational - horizon and granularity distinction, distinct from single-variable / single-author / interchangeable framings'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO02/APO05. Foundational tier. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a hotel group's five-year IT strategic plan. Which component is MOST essential?

options.A: A complete register of current vendors, contracts and renewal dates
options.B: A target state linked to corporate goals, with a prioritized roadmap
options.C: A detailed list of next year's projects with budgets and owners
options.D: An organization chart showing every IT role and reporting line

questions.key_concept: An IT strategic plan links a target state to enterprise goals and sets a prioritized multi-year roadmap to close the gaps.
questions.pre_read: Ask which component shows direction over the plan's full horizon.
questions.correct_explanation: A strategic plan must show where IT needs to be to support enterprise goals and how it will get there: a target state derived from those goals, a gap assessment against today, and a prioritized roadmap with measures. Option C is useful, but a one-year project list is tactical; it cannot show whether a five-year direction is aligned or achievable.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor records support operations and sourcing, but they describe current contracts, not where IT must go to support enterprise goals.
wrong_explanations.C: A one-year project list is a tactical plan. It cannot show the multi-year direction or how projects add up to the target state.
wrong_explanations.D: An organization chart shows current structure. It says nothing about direction, priorities or how IT will support enterprise goals.

tips: Eliminate: A and D describe current operations, not future direction.
Final two: B beats C because a strategic plan needs a goal-linked target state and roadmap; next year's project list is tactical.
Exam cue: for strategic plans, look for direction tied to enterprise goals; annual detail belongs to tactical planning.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); ISO/IEC 38500:2024 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT strategic plan components - 6 integrated elements distinct from vendor list / project list / org chart'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO02. questions.subtopic: IT Policy Hierarchy. Conflicting Local Procedure
questions.question: A business unit's backup procedure allows 30-day retention, but the corporate data retention standard requires 90 days. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor?

options.A: The procedure must conform to the standard, so this is a finding
options.B: The procedure governs because the business unit knows its own needs
options.C: Both documents are valid because each was approved by its own owner
options.D: The standard should be lowered to 30 days to remove the conflict

questions.key_concept: Procedures must conform to the standards and policies above them; a weaker local procedure is a compliance gap, not a valid alternative.
questions.pre_read: Place each document in the policy hierarchy before judging which requirement applies.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy documents form a hierarchy: procedures implement standards, and standards implement policy. A lower-level document cannot relax a higher-level requirement, so the 30-day procedure is noncompliant and should be reported, with management deciding how to align it or whether to grant a formal exception. Treating both as valid because each had an approver ignores the hierarchy and leaves two conflicting rules in force.

wrong_explanations.B: Local knowledge does not let a procedure override a corporate standard. A unit needing different retention must seek a formal, approved exception.
wrong_explanations.C: Separate approvals do not make conflicting documents both valid. Higher-level requirements prevail, so a weaker procedure is a compliance gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Retention periods follow legal and business needs that management sets. Lowering the standard to fit a noncompliant procedure reverses the hierarchy.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a local procedure override corporate requirements, and D bends the standard to fit the gap.
Final two: A beats C because lower-level documents must conform to higher ones; separate approvals do not legitimize a conflict.
Exam cue: in a document conflict, the higher level governs; report the gap and let management align it or approve an exception.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO01 (Managed I&T Management Framework); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Control A.5.1 (Policies for Information Security); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1008 (Criteria)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'information security management program structure - 8 integrated elements (strategy/architecture/controls/roles/operations/training/IR/metrics), distinct from tool list / single policy / attestation'. Public source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 + NIST CSF v2.0 + ISACA. All scenario specifics (regional savings bank) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Rebalanced (Oct 2026): re-angled from 2A2 to 2A3.

questions.question: An IT steering committee groups IT investments into run, grow and transform tiers. Which portfolio practice should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: Fund the run tier fully and transform from any leftovers
options.B: Rank every proposal by net present value in one pool
options.C: Drop the tiers to avoid funding disputes between teams
options.D: Set target funding ranges per tier based on strategy

questions.key_concept: Portfolio tiers work when each has a target funding range set by enterprise strategy and is judged with criteria suited to that tier.
questions.pre_read: Notice the committee already uses tiers. Ask which practice turns the tiers into a deliberate strategic funding decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Portfolio management balances investments against enterprise strategy. Target allocation ranges per tier make the run, grow and transform mix an explicit strategic choice, and each tier can then be judged with fitting criteria. Ranking everything by net present value looks rigorous, but transform initiatives rarely show early financial returns, so a single financial ranking starves strategic change and loses alignment.

wrong_explanations.A: Funding transformation only from leftovers makes strategic change an afterthought. The mix should be a deliberate choice, not a residual.
wrong_explanations.B: A single financial ranking ignores strategic posture. Long-horizon transform work loses to quick operational payback even when strategy needs it.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing tiers hides the strategic mix from the committee. Disputes are resolved by clear criteria, not by losing visibility.

tips: Eliminate: A makes transformation a residual, and C removes the visibility the tiers provide.
Final two: D beats B because strategy should set the investment mix; one financial ranking favors short-term payback over business alignment.
Exam cue: in portfolio questions, prefer the option where enterprise strategy sets the balance, not a single financial score.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT portfolio tier discipline - run/grow/transform with target allocation + tier-appropriate criteria, distinct from single-pool / run-only / tier-elimination'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO05. All scenario specifics (metropolitan transit authority) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A logistics company outsources IT operations to several providers. Which practice should the IS auditor consider MOST important for managing their service delivery?

options.A: An annual contract meeting to review pricing and renewal terms
options.B: Quarterly executive governance meetings focused on partnership trust
options.C: Ongoing SLA monitoring with periodic provider risk reassessment
options.D: Reliance on each provider's annual SOC 2 Type 2 report

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing transfers the work, not the accountability; the company must keep monitoring service levels and reassessing provider risk itself.
questions.pre_read: Notice the company remains accountable for outsourced services. Ask which practice gives it continuing evidence of performance and risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Accountability for outsourced services stays with the company. Ongoing SLA monitoring shows whether each provider delivers, and periodic risk reassessment catches changes in security, financial or operational exposure. A SOC 2 Type 2 report is valuable assurance, but it covers a fixed period and scope chosen with the provider, so relying on it alone leaves service performance and the company's own risks unmonitored.

wrong_explanations.A: An annual commercial review comes too late to catch service failures and focuses on price rather than delivery.
wrong_explanations.B: Governance meetings about the relationship build goodwill but produce no performance evidence or risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: A SOC 2 report is one input. It covers a set period and scope and does not measure SLA performance against the company's needs.

tips: Eliminate: A is an infrequent price review, and B builds relationships without measuring delivery.
Final two: C beats D because the company keeps accountability and needs its own ongoing evidence; a third-party report supplements monitoring rather than replacing it.
Exam cue: outsourcing never transfers accountability, so favor the option where the organization keeps monitoring.
