Public source: COBIT 2019 APO05. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Risk Register Tooling and Workflow Design
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the design of a new risk register tool at a bank. Which feature MOST supports the register's effectiveness over time?

options.A: Automated population of risks from incident and threat feeds
options.B: Lifecycle workflow with named owners and an audit trail
options.C: A simple shared spreadsheet maintained by the risk team
options.D: More than fifty mandatory data fields for each risk record

questions.key_concept: A register stays effective when each risk moves through a tracked lifecycle with a named owner and an audit trail of decisions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the phrase over time. Ask which feature keeps risks owned and updated after they are first recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: A register's value lies in risks being owned, treated and monitored, not just listed. Lifecycle workflow with a named owner and an audit trail keeps each risk moving and shows who decided what. Automated feeds add coverage and look efficient, but they cannot assess business impact or assign accountability, so the register fills up without being managed.

wrong_explanations.A: Feeds can suggest risks, but identification and assessment need business judgment. Automation without owners produces an unmanaged list.
wrong_explanations.C: A manual spreadsheet lacks workflow, ownership controls and change history, so it decays as the bank changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Excessive mandatory fields discourage updates. Complexity reduces adoption without improving ownership.

tips: Eliminate: C has no workflow or history, and D buries users in data entry.
Final two: B beats A because accountability keeps a register alive; automated feeds add entries but no owner or judgment.
Exam cue: for risk registers, choose ownership and lifecycle tracking over volume of data or automation.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk register tooling lifecycle workflow design, complements d2_021 (foundational risk register definition)'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A bank's management is building a compliance program covering FFIEC, GLBA, BSA/AML and CCPA. Which design BEST supports sustained compliance?

options.A: Separate compliance teams and controls for each regulation
options.B: One control library mapped to each regulation, with named owners
options.C: The strictest regulation applied to every process as the standard
options.D: Compliance fully outsourced to a managed service provider

questions.key_concept: Integrated compliance maps one control set to many regulations, with clear owners, so overlaps are tested once and gaps are visible.
questions.pre_read: Notice the many overlapping regulations. Ask which design avoids duplication while keeping each requirement traceable.
questions.correct_explanation: Many requirements overlap across these regulations. A single control library mapped to each one lets a control satisfy several obligations, makes gaps visible, and gives each area a named owner. Separate teams per regulation bring depth, but they duplicate controls and testing, burden the business with repeated requests, and can miss cross-regulation gaps no single team owns.

wrong_explanations.A: Siloed teams duplicate controls and testing, and gaps between regulations may fall to nobody.
wrong_explanations.C: Regulations differ in scope, not just strictness. One regulation's rules do not cover another's specific requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: Providers can support, but the bank remains accountable for compliance. Outsourcing does not transfer that accountability.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes one regulation covers the others, and D tries to outsource accountability.
Final two: B beats A because one mapped control set avoids duplication and exposes gaps, while silos repeat work and miss overlaps.
Exam cue: for multi-regulation compliance, choose a unified, mapped control framework with named owners.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance with External Requirements); ISO 37301:2021 (Compliance Management Systems); FFIEC IT Examination Handbook
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Compliance program multi-regulation operationalization - integrated with mapping, complements d2_050 (multi-sector regulatory mapping audit-design analysis) and d2_005 (GRC integration)'. Public source: FFIEC + COBIT 2019 MEA03. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a healthcare network's IT governance committees. Which structure MOST supports effective IT governance?

options.A: One weekly committee deciding strategy, risk, architecture and change
options.B: Several committees with shared members but no written charters
options.C: The CIO deciding every IT matter directly, without committees
options.D: Distinct chartered committees with decision rights and escalation

questions.key_concept: Effective IT governance assigns distinct decisions to distinct bodies, each with a charter, decision rights and escalation path.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words effective governance. Ask which structure makes clear who decides what, and how issues move up.
questions.correct_explanation: Strategy, risk, architecture and operational change need different members, cadences and authority. Distinct committees with chartered decision rights and escalation paths give each decision a clear owner and route issues to the right level. One combined committee seems efficient for coordination, but it mixes governance with operational decisions, overloads one agenda and blurs accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: One committee mixes strategic and operational decisions, overloads the agenda, and blurs who is accountable for what.
wrong_explanations.B: Without charters, decision rights and scope are unclear, so overlap and gaps grow.
wrong_explanations.C: Concentrating every decision in one executive removes oversight and stakeholder input that governance requires.

tips: Eliminate: B lacks charters and clear decision rights, and C removes oversight entirely.
Final two: D beats A because distinct, chartered bodies give each decision clear accountability; one committee mixes governance with management.
Exam cue: good governance structures have defined charters, decision rights and escalation paths.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Governance and Management Roles); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); ISO/IEC 38500:2024 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT governance committee structure beyond IT Steering Committee - purpose-distinct multi-committee architecture, complements d2_003/d2_054 (steering committee specifics)'. Public source: COBIT 2019. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Round 2 review (Oct 2026): framework_ref updated to ISO/IEC 38500:2024.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a credit union reviews new outsourcing contracts. Which exit provision MOST protects the credit union's long-term interests?

options.A: Exit terms agreed at signing for data, transition and handover
options.B: A right to terminate for convenience on 90 days' written notice
options.C: Exit planning deferred until termination becomes likely
options.D: No documented exit terms, to avoid signaling expected failure

questions.key_concept: Exit strategy is negotiated before signing, when leverage is greatest: data return, transition assistance and knowledge transfer.
questions.pre_read: Notice the contracts are new. Ask when the credit union has the most leverage to secure exit support.
questions.correct_explanation: Leverage is highest before signing. Agreeing exit terms then, covering data return formats, transition assistance and knowledge transfer, means the credit union can leave without losing data or service. A termination-for-convenience right lets it leave, but says nothing about how: without transition obligations, the vendor has little reason to help a departing customer.

wrong_explanations.B: A right to leave without transition support risks lost data and service gaps. Exit needs cooperation terms, not just termination rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Once termination is likely, leverage is gone and the vendor has little reason to cooperate.
wrong_explanations.D: Exit terms are prudent risk management, not a prediction of failure. Their absence leaves the credit union exposed.

tips: Eliminate: C waits until leverage is lost, and D leaves exit undefined.
Final two: A beats B because a right to leave is not a plan to leave; transition and data terms protect continuity.
Exam cue: plan the exit at the entrance; negotiate exit support before signing, when leverage is greatest.
questions.framework_ref: FFIEC Outsourcing Technology Services booklet; ISACA Outsourced IT Environments Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); ISO/IEC 27036-1:2021 (Cybersecurity — Supplier Relationships — Overview and Concepts)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Outsourcing exit strategy proactive planning at contract signing - distinct from d2_106 (vendor offboarding execution at relationship end)'. Public source: OCC Bulletin 2013-29 + ISACA Outsourcing Governance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a defense contractor reviews a new data loss prevention program. Which design feature MOST supports its effectiveness?

options.A: Blocking enforced on every egress channel regardless of context
options.B: Vendor default policies, left unchanged to reduce effort
options.C: Policies driven by data classification and tuned per channel
options.D: Monitoring of data flows with no enforcement action taken

questions.key_concept: DLP protects what is classified. Effective programs start with classification, then tune policies per channel to balance protection and usability.
questions.pre_read: Notice the program is new. Ask what DLP needs to know before it can decide what to block.
questions.correct_explanation: DLP can only protect data it can recognize, so classification comes first; policies are then tuned for email, endpoint and cloud channels and refined from false-positive analysis. Blanket blocking feels like the strongest protection for a defense contractor, but without classification it blocks legitimate work, floods analysts with alerts and drives users to unmonitored workarounds.

wrong_explanations.A: Context-free blocking disrupts legitimate work and drives users to workarounds, weakening protection overall.
wrong_explanations.B: Defaults do not reflect the contractor's own data or classification scheme, so sensitive data may go unrecognized.
wrong_explanations.D: Detection without enforcement lets sensitive data leave. It suits a tuning phase, not a mature program.

tips: Eliminate: B ignores the contractor's own data, and D watches data leave without stopping it.
Final two: C beats A because DLP must know what to protect; blanket blocking without classification disrupts work and invites workarounds.
Exam cue: for data protection controls, classification comes first; enforcement follows what is classified.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 (Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems); CSA Cloud Controls Matrix; COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'DLP program design - risk-based multi-element approach, no prior D2 coverage'. Public source: NIST SP 800-53 + CSA + ISACA Data Governance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An insurer's management plans to use a vendor's AI fraud model in claims processing. Which governance approach BEST addresses the third-party AI risk?

options.A: Reliance on the vendor's SOC 2 Type 2 report and model documentation
options.B: Independent testing on the insurer's data, plus output monitoring
options.C: In-house AI development instead, to remove vendor risk entirely
options.D: The same oversight applied to any packaged vendor software

questions.key_concept: The insurer stays accountable for AI outcomes. Third-party models need independent testing on its own data and ongoing output monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Notice the model makes decisions on the insurer's claims. Ask who is accountable if it is biased or inaccurate.
questions.correct_explanation: The insurer remains accountable for decisions the model drives, so it needs its own evidence: independent testing on its claims data for accuracy and bias, then ongoing monitoring for drift. A SOC 2 report and model documentation are useful vendor artifacts, but they cover the vendor's controls and claims, not how the model performs on this insurer's data.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor artifacts cover the vendor's controls, not model accuracy or bias on the insurer's data. Accountability cannot be outsourced.
wrong_explanations.C: In-house models carry the same model risks. Avoiding vendors does not remove the need for testing and monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: AI models drift and can embed bias, risks that standard software oversight does not test for.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes in-house AI carries no model risk, and D ignores drift and bias.
Final two: B beats A because the insurer is accountable for outcomes; vendor reports cover vendor controls, not performance on its data.
Exam cue: when a vendor supplies a decision model, look for independent validation and monitoring by the accountable business.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management System); COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Third-party AI/ML governance application - layered approach, complements d2_036 (IT-VMO structure) and d2_099 (vendor onboarding)'. Public source: NIST AI RMF + ISACA Auditing AI. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that 60% of a holding company's IT operations spend goes to one cloud provider. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Accept the concentration as the price of negotiated discounts
options.B: Diversify across three cloud providers at once, whatever the cost
options.C: Defer analysis until a provider failure actually occurs
options.D: Weigh failure scenarios against appetite, then treat any excess

questions.key_concept: Concentration risk is managed risk-based: quantify the exposure, compare it with appetite, and mitigate only where it exceeds tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem gives a number but no analysis. Ask what must happen before deciding whether to diversify.
questions.correct_explanation: Concentration is not automatically acceptable or unacceptable. The company should model failure, regulatory and exit scenarios, compare the exposure with risk appetite, and then mitigate where tolerance is exceeded, through exit readiness or selective diversification. Immediate multi-cloud diversification feels protective, but it commits major cost and complexity before anyone knows whether the risk warrants it.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting without analysis is not informed risk acceptance. Discounts do not offset an unmeasured exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Diversifying before assessment may add cost and complexity that exceed the risk itself. Treatment should follow analysis.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a failure means assessing the risk only after its impact has already occurred.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts an unmeasured exposure, and C waits for the failure to happen.
Final two: D beats B because treatment should follow assessment against appetite; diversifying first may cost more than the risk.
Exam cue: assess against appetite before treating; the risk-based answer measures first, then acts proportionately.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27036-1:2021 (Cybersecurity — Supplier Relationships — Overview and Concepts); COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Vendor concentration risk quantify-then-mitigate, no prior D2 coverage'. Public source: OCC Bulletin 2013-29 + FFIEC. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a media company reviews its Cloud Center of Excellence. Which role MOST supports cloud governance maturity?

options.A: Setting standards and guardrails, with teams managing their own usage
options.B: Provisioning each cloud resource centrally on behalf of every team
options.C: Advising teams on request, with no authority over any standards
options.D: Owning cloud security for every workload, replacing business units

questions.key_concept: A mature Cloud Center of Excellence enables: it sets standards and guardrails while teams manage their own consumption within them.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word maturity. Ask which role scales control across many teams without becoming a bottleneck.
questions.correct_explanation: A Cloud Center of Excellence matures governance by setting architecture standards, security baselines, cost guardrails and reusable patterns, while teams manage their own usage within those limits. Central provisioning gives tight control and looks safe, but it bottlenecks every team, slows the business and keeps accountability for consumption away from the people making the decisions.

wrong_explanations.B: Central provisioning creates a bottleneck and separates consumers from accountability for what they use.
wrong_explanations.C: Advice without authority cannot enforce baselines or cost discipline, so governance stays optional.
wrong_explanations.D: Security accountability stays with workload owners. A central team cannot be the sole defense for every business unit's workload.

tips: Eliminate: C has no authority to govern, and D strips workload owners of their accountability.
Final two: A beats B because guardrails with team-managed usage scale governance, while central provisioning bottlenecks teams and blurs accountability.
Exam cue: mature governance functions set guardrails and enable; they do not do every task themselves.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Cloud Computing Management Audit/Assurance Program; CSA Cloud Controls Matrix; COBIT 2019 APO03 (Managed Enterprise Architecture); COBIT 2019 APO13 (Managed Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud Center of Excellence governance - enabling function pattern, complements d2_087 (multi-cloud governance synthesis) and d2_100 (FinOps)'. Public source: ISACA Cloud Governance + CSA CCM. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a bank's IT incident management process. Which classification approach MOST supports consistent prioritization?

options.A: Categories by technology area, used to route each incident
options.B: Severity set by the business owner's judgment, without criteria
options.C: An impact-and-urgency matrix with defined criteria per tier
options.D: Incidents handled in the order in which they are reported

questions.key_concept: Consistent prioritization comes from a documented matrix of business impact and urgency, with defined criteria and response targets per tier.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word consistent. Ask which approach makes two engineers rate the same incident the same way, by business impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Priority should reflect business consequence and urgency, and consistency needs written criteria. A matrix of impact and urgency with defined criteria per tier gives every engineer the same answer for the same incident and links tiers to response targets. Technology categories are useful for routing to the right team, but they say nothing about business impact, so they cannot set priority.

wrong_explanations.A: Technology categories decide who responds, not how urgently. Without an impact dimension, a minor and a critical outage rank the same.
wrong_explanations.B: Undocumented judgment, even a business owner's, varies between people and shifts, so the same incident gets different priorities.
wrong_explanations.D: Arrival order ignores impact, so a critical outage can wait behind minor requests.

tips: Eliminate: B depends on undocumented judgment, and D ignores impact altogether.
Final two: C beats A because priority must reflect business impact; technology categories route incidents but do not rank them.
Exam cue: prioritization questions favor business impact with documented criteria over technical category or arrival order.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Incident Management; COBIT 2019 DSS02 (Managed Service Requests and Incidents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT incident classification multi-dimensional severity matrix - complements d2_105 (incident response escalation analysis) and d2_110 (crisis communication)'. Public source: ITIL 4 + FFIEC. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Management at a bank operating in several US states and the EU wants to anticipate regulatory change. Which approach BEST supports this objective?

options.A: Respond to each regulation once it is finalized and effective
options.B: Rely on external counsel to flag changes it judges material
options.C: Assign staff to track proposed rules and feed them into planning
options.D: Adopt the strictest draft rule everywhere as soon as it is published

questions.key_concept: Proactive compliance needs internal, accountable horizon scanning: named staff watching proposed rules, with results feeding planning.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word anticipate. Ask which option keeps accountability inside the bank and acts before rules become final.
questions.correct_explanation: Anticipating regulatory change means watching proposed rules and consultations before they are final, with named staff tracking each regulator and the results fed into planning. External counsel adds expertise, but relying on it leaves coverage to whatever counsel chooses to flag. Management, not an adviser, remains accountable for systematic monitoring across the whole regulatory perimeter.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting until rules are final and effective is reactive. It compresses the implementation window and removes any chance to plan or comment early.
wrong_explanations.B: Counsel is a useful input, but it reports only what it judges material. Coverage is unsystematic and accountability for monitoring moves outside the bank.
wrong_explanations.D: Applying every draft rule everywhere at once over-complies where drafts may change or never take effect, wasting resources without a risk-based case.

tips: Eliminate: A is purely reactive, and D over-complies with drafts that may never take effect.
Final two: C beats B because accountability for monitoring stays with management and feeds planning, while counsel only reports what it chooses.
Exam cue: when an option hands an ongoing governance duty to an outside party, look for the one that keeps internal ownership.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance with External Requirements); ISO 37301:2021 (Compliance Management Systems)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Regulatory horizon scanning proactive compliance, complements d2_113 (compliance program operationalization)'. Public source: FFIEC + ISACA Compliance Management. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A California resident visiting the EU submits access and deletion requests to an e-commerce company covered by both CCPA and GDPR. How should the privacy officer BEST respond?

options.A: Apply both laws together and document the basis used
options.B: Handle the request under GDPR alone as the stricter regime
options.C: Apply CCPA alone, because California residence decides the governing law
options.D: Ask the consumer to resubmit after returning to California

questions.key_concept: When two privacy regimes apply to one request, satisfy the union of obligations, meet the shorter deadline and document the dual basis.
questions.pre_read: Notice both laws can apply at once. Ask which option meets every obligation rather than choosing one regime.
questions.correct_explanation: Both regimes can apply: CCPA through the consumer's California residence, and GDPR through the company's EU establishment or its targeting of people in the EU. The defensible response meets the shorter deadline, satisfies both sets of access and deletion duties, and records the dual basis. GDPR alone looks safe because it is often stricter, but it can miss CCPA-specific duties, such as its rules for verifying the consumer's identity.

wrong_explanations.B: GDPR is often stricter, but not on every point. One regime alone can miss CCPA duties, such as its consumer-verification rules, and leaves no record of dual compliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Residence does not switch GDPR off. GDPR can apply through the company's EU establishment or processing, so ignoring it creates exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Refusing or delaying a valid rights request breaches both laws' response obligations. Administrative burden is not a lawful reason to decline.

tips: Eliminate: C wrongly assumes residence alone decides the law, and D refuses a valid rights request.
Final two: A beats B because meeting both regimes and documenting the basis leaves no gap, while one 'stricter' regime can still miss duties.
Exam cue: when several regulations apply, the answer usually satisfies all of them, not the one that looks strictest.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Multi-jurisdiction GDPR/CCPA data-subject-rights conflict synthesis - both-apply-with-union, complements d2_066 (multi-jurisdiction privacy program scaling) and d2_107 (GDPR vs SOX)'. questions.question: A bank's analysis shows concentration on one cloud provider exceeds risk appetite; the CIO plans to accept the excess to keep discounts. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: CIO accepts the excess as owner of the provider relationship
options.B: IS auditor signs off the acceptance after testing the analysis
options.C: Accept it without record, given the provider's strong reliability
options.D: Escalate to senior management to treat or formally accept it

questions.key_concept: Risk above appetite must be escalated to senior management to treat or formally accept; operational owners and auditors cannot accept it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the analysis is done and exposure exceeds appetite. Ask who has authority to accept that excess.
questions.correct_explanation: Exposure above appetite cannot be accepted by the function that manages the relationship. Senior management, as risk owner within board-set appetite, must decide whether to treat the excess or formally accept it, with the decision documented. The CIO owns the provider relationship, so acceptance looks natural, but an operational owner accepting above-appetite risk to protect discounts overrides the board's appetite without authority.

wrong_explanations.A: The CIO manages the relationship but cannot accept risk beyond board-set appetite; that decision sits with senior management.
wrong_explanations.B: Auditors assess and report risk. Signing off acceptance makes the auditor part of management's decision and impairs independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Unrecorded acceptance bypasses governance, and past reliability does not reduce the impact of a provider failure.

tips: Eliminate: B puts the auditor in management's decision, and C accepts the risk without any record.
Final two: D beats A because above-appetite risk is accepted by senior management, not the operational owner protecting discounts.
Exam cue: when exposure exceeds appetite, look for escalation to the accountable risk owner, not acceptance lower down.

questions.subtopic: IT Policy Hierarchy. Policy vs Standard Altitude
questions.question: A draft information security policy lists required password lengths, approved encryption algorithms and firewall port numbers. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Keep the details in the policy so staff find everything together
options.B: Move the technical settings into standards that the policy references
options.C: Delete the technical settings entirely, since the engineers already know them
options.D: Have the board approve each technical setting when it changes

questions.key_concept: Policies state high-level intent and stay stable; mandatory technical specifics belong in standards that support the policy.
questions.pre_read: Ask how often each detail would change, and which document level is built to change at that pace.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy states management's intent and direction, so it should change rarely and be approved at a senior level. Settings such as password lengths and port numbers change often and belong in standards, which make the policy measurable and can be updated without re-approving it. Keeping them in the policy feels convenient, but every technical change would then force a full policy revision and approval cycle.

wrong_explanations.A: Mixing settings into the policy makes it unstable. Every technology change would trigger a full policy revision and senior approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Undocumented settings cannot be enforced or audited consistently. Mandatory technical requirements must be written down, just at the standard level.
wrong_explanations.D: The board sets direction and approves policy. Approving individual technical settings is management detail that would overload governance and slow change.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves mandatory settings undocumented, and D drags the board into technical detail.
Final two: B beats A because policy stays stable at the intent level while standards carry settings that change often.
Exam cue: policy says what and why; standards set mandatory specifics; procedures say how; guidelines advise.

questions.question: A health insurer's benefits SaaS vendor reports a breach but cannot yet confirm whether the insurer's data was affected. What should the IS auditor advise the insurer to do FIRST?

options.A: Activate internal incident response and assess notification duties
options.B: Wait until the vendor's investigation confirms the full breach scope
options.C: Send the insurer's own team to run the vendor's investigation
options.D: Notify every member now that their data may be exposed

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing a service does not outsource accountability; the insurer must start its own response and assess its own notification duties.
questions.pre_read: Notice the facts are incomplete. Ask what the accountable organization can do now without waiting or overreacting.
questions.correct_explanation: The insurer remains accountable for its members' data even when a vendor processes it. It should start its own incident response now: enforce contractual notification rights, assess its HIPAA notification obligations with counsel, and plan communications while documenting the timeline. Waiting for the vendor feels prudent because facts are uncertain, but the insurer's own obligations and timelines may already be running.

wrong_explanations.B: Waiting hands control of the timeline to the vendor. The insurer's own notification obligations and deadlines may already be running.
wrong_explanations.C: Contracts rarely allow the customer to take over a vendor's investigation. Doing so oversteps rights and may disrupt evidence handling.
wrong_explanations.D: Notifying members before scope is known risks inaccurate communication. Notification should follow an assessment of who is actually affected.

tips: Eliminate: C oversteps contractual rights, and D notifies members before knowing who is affected.
Final two: A beats B because accountability for the data stays with the insurer, so its own response cannot wait for the vendor.
Exam cue: when a vendor has an incident, the outsourcing organization keeps accountability and starts its own response.
questions.framework_ref: HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.400-414); NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management)

questions.subtopic: Data Classification + Retention + Privacy Multi-Control Synthesis
questions.question: For a FinTech's new data architecture, executives propose treating all customer data as sensitive and retaining everything for seven years. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Treat every customer record as sensitive under maximum controls
options.B: Keep every record for seven years to satisfy regulators
options.C: Classify data in tiers and set retention per category
options.D: Require explicit consent before collecting any customer data

questions.key_concept: Data classification is the foundation: tiers drive proportionate protection, and retention follows each category's legal and business requirement.
questions.pre_read: Notice the proposals are flat rules for all data. Ask which option lets controls follow the actual risk of each category.
questions.correct_explanation: Tiered classification is the foundation of data governance: it lets protection, retention and privacy controls follow the real sensitivity and legal requirements of each category. Retention can then be set per category, avoiding storage-limitation breaches. Requiring consent for all collection sounds privacy-friendly, but consent is only one lawful basis and is often not the right one; it does not address classification or retention at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Uniform maximum controls ignore actual sensitivity, raising cost without proportionate benefit. Controls should follow classification tiers.
wrong_explanations.B: A flat seven-year period keeps some data longer than needed, breaching storage limitation, and may keep other data too briefly.
wrong_explanations.D: Consent is only one lawful basis and is often inappropriate. It also leaves classification and retention unaddressed.

tips: Eliminate: A applies costly controls regardless of sensitivity, and B breaches storage limitation with a flat retention period.
Final two: C beats D because classification is the foundation that drives protection and retention; consent is one lawful basis, not a design.
Exam cue: when proposals apply one rule to all data, look for the option that classifies first.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); DAMA-DMBOK 2nd Edition; ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (Privacy Information Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Data discipline multi-control synthesis - tiered-per-purpose approach, complements d2_098 (multi-regulation retention design) and d2_063 (privacy operationalization)'. Public source: GDPR Article 5 + ISACA Data Governance + DAMA-DMBOK. All scenario specifics (FinTech rollout, four leader positions in tension) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Risk Treatment Trade-Offs Across Multiple Risks
questions.question: A CISO proposes spending most of a $1M treatment budget on the lowest-impact of three risks. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Approve the CISO's allocation as the domain expert's judgment
options.B: Formally accept each of the three risks and reallocate the budget
options.C: Redirect most of the funding to the highest-impact risk
options.D: Compare expected-loss reduction per dollar against risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Treatment budgets should follow expected-loss reduction per dollar, measured against risk appetite, not expert preference or impact alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the budget is fixed and three risks compete. Ask which option weighs both likelihood and treatment effectiveness.
questions.correct_explanation: With a fixed budget, the sound approach is to quantify each risk's expected loss, estimate how much each treatment would reduce it, and compare the reduction per dollar against risk appetite. The allocation is then revised with a documented rationale and risk-function sign-off. Moving money to the highest-impact risk looks intuitive, but impact alone ignores likelihood and how effective each treatment actually is.

wrong_explanations.A: Deferring to expertise skips independent analysis. The proposal favors the lowest-impact risk, which is exactly what needs testing.
wrong_explanations.B: Accepting all three risks without analysis abandons treatment of exposures that may exceed appetite, and partial treatment is not formal acceptance.
wrong_explanations.C: Impact alone ignores likelihood and treatment effectiveness. The largest risk may not deliver the greatest loss reduction per dollar.

tips: Eliminate: A skips independent analysis, and B abandons treatment without checking appetite.
Final two: D beats C because risk-based allocation weighs likelihood and treatment effect, not impact alone.
Exam cue: when choosing among risks for limited funds, prefer the option that quantifies risk reduction against appetite.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); ISACA Risk IT Framework; FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk treatment trade-offs across multiple risks - per-dollar expected-loss reduction analysis, complements d2_089 (constrained-budget tiered prioritization) and d2_070 (multi-option treatment scenario)'. Public source: ISO 31000:2018 + ISACA Risk IT + FAIR. All scenario specifics (regional retailer, three competing risks, $1M budget, holiday-season urgency) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A bank has six weeks to assess a FinTech acquisition target with sparse documentation and two disclosed security incidents. Which due diligence approach is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor?

options.A: Review the system inventory now and defer depth until closing
options.B: Go deep on critical systems, incident root causes and deal-breakers
options.C: Treat the two disclosed incidents as automatic deal-breakers
options.D: Rely on the transaction adviser's IT due diligence report

questions.key_concept: IT due diligence under time pressure is risk-based: focus depth on critical systems, incident root causes and clear deal-breaker criteria.
questions.pre_read: Notice the short window and the incidents. Ask which option puts limited time where the deal risk is greatest.
questions.correct_explanation: With limited time and sparse documentation, due diligence must be risk-based: concentrate effort on regulatory-critical systems, find the root causes of the disclosed incidents and agree deal-breaker criteria before the board votes. Relying on the transaction adviser looks efficient, but the adviser serves the deal and the bank stays accountable for its own judgment on IT risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Deferring depth until after closing means risks are discovered when the bank already owns them and can no longer price or decline.
wrong_explanations.C: Incidents matter, but their root cause and remediation decide the risk. An automatic rejection ignores evidence that may be favorable.
wrong_explanations.D: An adviser's report is a useful input, but the bank stays accountable for the decision and needs its own risk-focused view.

tips: Eliminate: A finds risks only after the bank owns them, and C rejects the deal without examining root causes.
Final two: B beats D because the bank stays accountable for the decision; an adviser's report supports it but cannot replace it.
Exam cue: with limited time, the answer focuses depth where risk is greatest rather than covering everything lightly.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk); OCC Comptroller's Licensing Manual — Business Combinations; FFIEC IT Examination Handbook
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Acquisition target IT due diligence depth-by-criticality, complements d2_104 (failed M&A integration synthesis at post-deal stage)'. questions.subtopic: Cloud Cost vs Availability Trade-Off Analysis
questions.question: A SaaS firm's single-region platform serves enterprise clients with 99.99% SLAs and self-serve users with none. Which architecture should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Run active-active across regions for every customer tier
options.B: Match each tier's resilience investment to its SLA and revenue
options.C: Stay single-region and accept 99.95 percent as close enough
options.D: Run active-passive across regions for every tier with fast failover

questions.key_concept: Availability investment should follow business value: resilience matched to each customer tier's SLA commitments and revenue.
questions.pre_read: Notice the tiers have very different commitments. Ask which option spends on resilience where the business needs it.
questions.correct_explanation: Resilience spending should follow business value. Enterprise clients with 99.99% SLAs justify multi-region active-active, while self-serve users with no SLA can stay single-region with better operations. Uniform active-passive looks like a balanced compromise, but it overspends on the self-serve tier and its failover time may still breach the 99.99% enterprise commitment.

wrong_explanations.A: Uniform active-active pays the highest cost for tiers that have no SLA and generate little revenue. Spending is not aligned to value.
wrong_explanations.C: Staying single-region leaves the 99.99% enterprise SLA unmet. Accepting a known contractual shortfall is not a defensible position.
wrong_explanations.D: One mode for all tiers overspends where no SLA exists, and active-passive failover time may still break the 99.99% enterprise SLA.

tips: Eliminate: A overspends on every tier, and C knowingly misses the enterprise SLA.
Final two: B beats D because investment should follow each tier's business value, not one compromise applied everywhere.
Exam cue: when customers or systems differ in value, prefer the option that tiers controls to match, not a uniform design.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Cloud Computing Management Audit/Assurance Program; CSA Cloud Controls Matrix; COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity)

questions.subtopic: Information Security Strategy Alignment with Business Strategy Synthesis
questions.question: Before board endorsement, an IS auditor finds a CISO's security strategy is a generic protect-detect-respond plan that never mentions the firm's acquisition and expansion plans. What is the auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Revise it to map capabilities to each business goal
options.B: Benchmark the plan against peer maturity scores and close the largest gaps
options.C: Rebuild the plan around the top threats in the latest threat assessment
options.D: Reject it and commission a complete rewrite from scratch

questions.key_concept: A security strategy must support business objectives; fix a generic plan by mapping capabilities to each business goal with measurable criteria.
questions.pre_read: Notice the strategy is generic, not wrong. Ask which option creates alignment without wasting the sound parts.
questions.correct_explanation: Security strategy exists to support business objectives, so each business goal needs matching capabilities, such as privacy and compliance for expansion and an integration playbook for acquisitions, each with measurable criteria. A full rewrite also produces alignment, but it discards sound protect-detect-respond content and delays the strategy, when targeted revision fixes the actual gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Peer benchmarks show where others are mature, not what this firm's expansion and acquisitions need, so closing gaps blindly can fund the wrong capabilities.
wrong_explanations.C: Threat-driven planning is still generic to the business. It ignores what expansion and acquisitions require, so alignment remains missing.
wrong_explanations.D: A rewrite discards sound content and delays delivery. The flaw is missing linkage, which targeted revision can address.

tips: Eliminate: B measures against peers, not this firm's goals, and C plans around threats while still ignoring business goals.
Final two: A beats D because the gap is alignment, which revision fixes without discarding sound work.
Exam cue: when a plan is sound but unaligned, choose the option that connects it to business objectives rather than scrapping it.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); COBIT 2019 APO13 (Managed Security); ISACA Information Security Management Audit/Assurance Program; ISO/IEC 27014 (Governance of Information Security)

questions.subtopic: SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3. Selection
questions.question: An IS auditor at a bank must rely on a critical SaaS vendor's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Which report is MOST appropriate to request?

options.A: SOC 1 Type 2 report on controls relevant to financial reporting
options.B: SOC 3 general-use report summarizing the vendor's controls
options.C: Internal audit report issued by the vendor's own audit team
options.D: SOC 2 Type 2 report on the relevant Trust Services Criteria

questions.key_concept: SOC 2 Type 2 covers the Trust Services Criteria over a period with detailed test results, so it supports audit reliance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word rely. Ask which report covers these criteria and also shows the tests performed.
questions.correct_explanation: A SOC 2 Type 2 report covers the Trust Services Criteria, including security, availability and confidentiality, and describes the service auditor's tests and results over a period. That detail is what an auditor needs to rely on the controls. A SOC 3 report addresses the same criteria, but it is a general-use summary without test details, so it cannot support reliance.

wrong_explanations.A: SOC 1 addresses controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting, not the security, availability and confidentiality objectives here.
wrong_explanations.B: SOC 3 is a general-use summary without detailed tests and results. It suits marketing, not audit reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: A vendor's own internal audit lacks independence from the vendor and follows no attestation standard, so reliance is weak.

tips: Eliminate: A covers financial reporting controls, and C lacks independence from the vendor.
Final two: D beats B because reliance needs detailed tests and results, which only the restricted SOC 2 report provides.
Exam cue: when the auditor must rely on a service provider's controls, choose the independent report with detailed test results.
questions.framework_ref: AICPA SSAE 18 AT-C 105 (Concepts Common to All Attestation Engagements); AICPA SSAE 18 AT-C 205 (Examination Engagements); AICPA Trust Services Criteria
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SOC report selection - matching audit objective to report scope, complements d2_057 (cloud risk continuous evidence with SOC 2)'. Public source: AICPA SSAE 18 + Trust Services Criteria. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Management at a SaaS company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification to meet enterprise customer demands. Which approach BEST supports this goal?

options.A: Hire a consultant to write the documents the certifier will review
options.B: Publicly declare alignment with the standard instead of certifying
options.C: Operate a risk-based ISMS, then engage an accredited certifier
options.D: Present the SOC 2 report to customers as an equivalent certificate

questions.key_concept: ISO/IEC 27001 certification rests on an operating ISMS: scope, risk assessment, Statement of Applicability, internal audit and management review.
questions.pre_read: Notice what enterprise customers want: assurance. Ask which option produces an ISMS that works, not just paperwork.
questions.correct_explanation: Certification is valuable only when it reflects an ISMS that actually operates: defined scope, risk assessment, controls selected in a Statement of Applicability, internal audit and management review, followed by an accredited body's Stage 1, Stage 2 and surveillance audits. Consultant-written documentation is tempting, but certification auditors test whether the ISMS operates, and paperwork alone gives customers no real assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Documents without operation fail Stage 2, which tests whether the ISMS works in practice. Management also stays accountable for the system.
wrong_explanations.B: Self-declared alignment carries no independent assurance and does not meet customers' certification requirement.
wrong_explanations.D: SOC 2 is an attestation report, not an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate. Presenting it as equivalent misleads customers.

tips: Eliminate: B offers no independent assurance, and D misrepresents a different report as a certificate.
Final two: C beats A because certification tests an operating ISMS that management owns, not documents written for the audit.
Exam cue: when an option aims to pass the audit rather than run the control, it is rarely the BEST answer.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems); ISACA Information Security Management Audit/Assurance Program
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ISO/IEC 27001 certification operationalization - real ISMS vs documentation-only, no prior D2 coverage'. Public source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a manufacturer reviews a proposed cyber-insurance program. Which design feature MOST supports its value as a risk-transfer mechanism?

options.A: Buy the highest limit available, whatever the actual exposure
options.B: Select the carrier offering the lowest premium for broad cover
options.C: Align policy terms with the incident response and notification process
options.D: Size limits and retention to the quantified loss exposure

questions.key_concept: Cyber insurance transfers risk effectively only when limits and retention are calibrated to quantified exposure and the firm's absorption capacity.
questions.pre_read: Notice the phrase risk transfer. Ask which feature decides how much of the actual loss is transferred.
questions.correct_explanation: Insurance transfers risk only to the extent the policy matches the exposure. Limits sized to a quantified loss analysis, and a retention the firm can absorb, determine how much loss actually moves to the insurer. Aligning terms with incident response and notification matters for claims, but it cannot fix a policy that is sized wrongly for the firm's exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Maximum limits regardless of exposure overpay for cover that may never be needed. Insurance should be calibrated, not maximized.
wrong_explanations.B: Cyber policies differ materially in exclusions and terms. Choosing on premium alone risks gaps exactly where losses occur.
wrong_explanations.C: Alignment with incident processes supports claims, but it does not decide how much of the exposure the policy actually covers.

tips: Eliminate: A overbuys cover regardless of exposure, and B ignores material differences in policy terms.
Final two: D beats C because transfer value depends first on covering the quantified exposure; process alignment supports claims.
Exam cue: when evaluating a risk response, ask whether it is calibrated to the measured risk.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk); ISACA Risk IT Framework; FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cyber insurance program design - calibration to risk profile, no prior D2 coverage'. Public source: ISACA Cyber Insurance guidance + FAIR. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Investment Portfolio. Board Reporting Dashboard
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the IT investment portfolio dashboard the CIO presents to the board each quarter. Which feature MOST supports board oversight?

options.A: Category view of business outcomes and realized benefits
options.B: Task-level Gantt charts for every active IT project
options.C: A single on-time, on-budget score covering the whole portfolio
options.D: A progress summary that omits projects flagged at risk

questions.key_concept: Board-level portfolio reporting is outcome-focused: investment categories, business benefits realized and flagged exceptions, at governance altitude.
questions.pre_read: Notice the audience is the board. Ask which option shows whether investments deliver business value.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's role is to ensure IT investments deliver value, so its dashboard should show the portfolio by category, such as run, grow and transform, with business outcomes, realized benefits and flagged exceptions. A single on-time, on-budget score is board-level and concise, but it measures delivery efficiency only and says nothing about whether investments are producing the intended benefits.

wrong_explanations.B: Task-level detail is management altitude. It buries the board in operations and hides portfolio-level value and risk.
wrong_explanations.C: One delivery score hides which investments are at risk and ignores whether benefits are realized, which is the board's core concern.
wrong_explanations.D: Omitting at-risk projects removes the very exceptions the board needs to act on and gives false assurance.

tips: Eliminate: B is management-level detail, and D hides the exceptions the board must see.
Final two: A beats C because board oversight is about value delivered, not just on-time, on-budget delivery.
Exam cue: for board reporting, prefer outcomes and exceptions at summary level over activity detail or a single efficiency number.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio)

questions.question: An IS auditor at a bank reviews how management assigns third-party vendors to risk tiers. Which criteria set is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Vendor size, measured by revenue and headcount
options.B: Data sensitivity, service criticality and regulatory impact
options.C: Scores from each vendor's most recent security self-assessment
options.D: Annual contract value and total spend with the vendor

questions.key_concept: Vendor tiering rests on inherent risk: the sensitivity of data handled, service criticality and regulatory impact, with documented thresholds.
questions.pre_read: Notice the task is tiering, which comes before assessment. Ask which criteria describe the risk the relationship creates.
questions.correct_explanation: Tiering decides how much oversight each vendor receives, so it must reflect the inherent risk of the relationship: the sensitivity of data handled, how critical the service is, and regulatory implications, with documented thresholds. Self-assessment scores look risk-focused, but they describe the vendor's claimed controls, which belong to the later assessment step and are not independently verified.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor size says nothing about the data or service involved. A small vendor can hold the most sensitive data.
wrong_explanations.C: Self-assessment scores reflect the vendor's own view of its controls. They inform residual risk after tiering, not the tier itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Spend does not equal risk. A low-cost vendor may process critical data or support a key regulated service.

tips: Eliminate: A and D use size and spend, which do not reflect the data or service a vendor touches.
Final two: B beats C because tiers follow inherent risk; self-assessed control scores come later and are unverified.
Exam cue: when sorting third parties by risk, look for criteria about data, criticality and regulation, not size or spend.

questions.question: An IS auditor is evaluating how the CIO measures IT-business alignment. Which metric BEST demonstrates alignment?

options.A: IT cost per ticket, project delivery and system availability
options.B: Number of monthly meetings between the CIO and business leaders
options.C: Share of IT investments tied to approved business objectives
options.D: Ratio of IT staff to total enterprise headcount

questions.key_concept: Alignment is measured by linkage: the share of IT investment traced to business objectives and outcomes, not IT efficiency.
questions.pre_read: Notice the question is about alignment, not performance. Ask which metric shows IT doing the right things for the business.
questions.correct_explanation: Alignment means IT effort and investment support the enterprise's objectives, so the strongest measure traces investments to approved business objectives and outcomes. Efficiency metrics such as cost per ticket and availability are valuable and measurable, but they show IT doing things right, not doing the right things. An efficient IT function can still invest in work the business does not need.

wrong_explanations.A: Efficiency metrics measure how well IT operates, not whether its work supports business objectives. Efficient IT can still be misaligned.
wrong_explanations.B: Meeting counts measure activity, not outcomes. Frequent meetings do not show that IT investment supports business goals.
wrong_explanations.D: Staffing ratios reflect structure and cost, not whether IT delivers what the business needs.

tips: Eliminate: B counts meetings rather than results, and D measures staffing structure, not alignment.
Final two: C beats A because alignment is about doing the right things for the business; efficiency only shows doing things right.
Exam cue: for alignment questions, pick the metric that links IT to business objectives over internal IT performance.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery); COBIT 2019 (Goals Cascade and Performance Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT-business alignment metrics - direct linkage measures, complements d2_004 (IT-business strategy alignment application)'. questions.question: A bank's CISO is designing security KPIs for executive management. Which design feature MOST supports executive-level security governance?

options.A: Control effectiveness and risk trends with escalation thresholds
options.B: Counts of alerts, incidents and vulnerabilities found each month
options.C: A single composite score combining every security dimension
options.D: Percentile rankings against peer banks on security maturity

questions.key_concept: Executive security KPIs are outcome-based: control effectiveness and risk exposure against objectives, with thresholds that trigger escalation.
questions.pre_read: Notice the audience is executives who govern. Ask which feature tells them when to act.
questions.correct_explanation: Executives govern security by knowing whether controls work and whether risk exposure stays within appetite. Outcome measures of control effectiveness and risk trends, with thresholds that trigger escalation, support that decision-making directly. Peer benchmarks add useful context, but they show relative standing, not whether the bank's own objectives and risk appetite are being met.

wrong_explanations.B: Volume counts show activity, not effectiveness. A rise in alerts may mean better detection or more attacks, so executives cannot act on it.
wrong_explanations.C: A single composite hides which dimension is failing, so executives cannot see where to intervene.
wrong_explanations.D: Benchmarks give relative position, but peers may share the same weaknesses. They do not measure exposure against the bank's appetite.

tips: Eliminate: B measures activity rather than outcomes, and C hides which area is failing.
Final two: A beats D because governance measures performance against the bank's own objectives and appetite, not peer position.
Exam cue: for executive metrics, prefer outcome measures tied to objectives and thresholds over volumes, composites or rankings.

questions.question: An IS auditor is helping the audit committee chair plan the year's IT agenda. Which approach BEST balances oversight depth with limited meeting time?

options.A: One comprehensive IT review at a single meeting each year
options.B: Private briefings between the chair and the CIO between meetings
options.C: Referral of IT topics to the full board instead
options.D: Standing IT risk updates each meeting, plus rotating deep dives

questions.key_concept: Effective committee IT oversight is layered: brief standing risk updates every meeting plus scheduled deep dives on rotating topics.
questions.pre_read: Notice the two goals, depth and limited time. Ask which option gives both continuity and depth.
questions.correct_explanation: A layered agenda gives the committee continuous visibility and depth: a short IT risk and incident update at every meeting, regular program updates, and rotating deep dives on topics such as security, privacy and resilience. A single annual review offers depth, but it leaves the committee without visibility for most of the year, so emerging risks reach it late.

wrong_explanations.A: One annual session gives depth once, but leaves the committee blind to emerging IT risks for the rest of the year.
wrong_explanations.B: Private chair briefings bypass the committee's collective oversight and leave other members without the information they need.
wrong_explanations.C: IT risk affects financial reporting and controls, which sit within the committee's remit. Passing it to the board removes focused oversight.

tips: Eliminate: B bypasses collective oversight, and C removes IT from the committee's remit.
Final two: D beats A because oversight must be continuous; an annual review leaves risks unseen for months.
Exam cue: for committee or board oversight, prefer a regular, structured cadence over one-off reviews or informal channels.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a medical-device maker reviews how the IT quality program categorizes its costs. Which structure BEST supports quality investment decisions?

options.A: A single total quality-spend line reported to executives
options.B: Testing and appraisal costs tracked apart from other spend
options.C: Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs
options.D: Quality spend as a share of IT budget, reported to the board

questions.key_concept: The cost-of-quality model separates prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure, showing where investment lowers total quality cost.
questions.pre_read: Notice the purpose is investment decisions. Ask which structure shows where spending more would reduce losses.
questions.correct_explanation: The cost-of-quality model shows how prevention and appraisal spending reduces internal and external failure costs, so management can see where more investment lowers total cost; for a medical-device maker, external failures carry regulatory and patient-safety consequences. A budget share reported to the board looks like a tidy governance metric, but it is one aggregate number that cannot show whether money prevents failures or pays for them.

wrong_explanations.A: One total line cannot show which category drives cost, so it cannot guide where to invest.
wrong_explanations.B: Tracking appraisal alone ignores prevention returns and the failure costs, including regulatory consequences, that matter most here.
wrong_explanations.D: A budget share is one aggregate number. It cannot show whether spending prevents failures or pays for them, so it cannot guide where to invest.

tips: Eliminate: A gives one undifferentiated number, and B omits prevention and failure costs.
Final two: C beats D because a budget share hides which cost category drives losses; the four-category split shows where prevention spending pays off.
Exam cue: when a question asks what supports investment decisions, prefer the structure that links spending to the losses it prevents.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 9004; COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality); Crosby Quality is Free; Juran Quality Handbook

Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): runner-up explanation teaches why a budget share fails.

questions.question: An IS auditor is testing a SaaS company's GDPR cross-border transfer compliance. Which procedure provides the MOST reliable evidence?

options.A: Review the board-approved privacy policy's description of transfers
options.B: Trace sampled data flows to their mechanism and safeguards
options.C: Confirm the transfer inventory lists SCCs for each data recipient
options.D: Inspect customer consent forms used as the basis for transfers

questions.key_concept: Reliable transfer evidence comes from testing actual data flows against documented mechanisms and supplementary measures, not from documents alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the phrase most reliable evidence. Ask which procedure tests what actually happens to the data.
questions.correct_explanation: Reliable evidence comes from testing implementation. Tracing a sample of actual data flows to their documented mechanism, such as SCCs with a transfer impact assessment, an adequacy decision or BCRs, and to any supplementary measures, shows whether transfers really comply. An inventory check confirms mechanisms are documented, but undocumented flows and missing safeguards would go undetected.

wrong_explanations.A: A board-approved policy still states intent, not practice. It cannot show whether actual transfers rely on a valid mechanism.
wrong_explanations.C: An inventory shows what is documented, not what happens. Flows missing from it, or lacking supplementary measures, would be missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Consent is a narrow derogation for transfers, not the normal basis. Reviewing forms does not test the main mechanisms.

tips: Eliminate: A reviews intent rather than practice, and D tests a narrow derogation instead of the main mechanisms.
Final two: B beats C because testing actual flows gives stronger evidence than confirming a list is complete on paper.
Exam cue: for MOST reliable evidence, prefer procedures that test what actually happens over reviews of documents.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Articles 44-50 (Transfers); EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on Supplementary Measures; CJEU Schrems II Judgment (C-311/18); Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 (Standard Contractual Clauses); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)

questions.subtopic: IT Change Management vs Enterprise Change Management
questions.question: A manufacturer's ERP rollout will change both its systems and how staff work. Which view of IT and enterprise change management should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: They are two names for the same governance discipline
options.B: They are distinct, complementary disciplines the rollout needs
options.C: IT change control should lead, as the rollout is mainly technical
options.D: Enterprise change management makes IT change control unnecessary

questions.key_concept: IT change management controls technical changes; enterprise change management drives people adoption. Major initiatives need both to deliver value.
questions.pre_read: Notice the rollout changes both systems and how people work. Ask which view covers both kinds of change.
questions.correct_explanation: IT change management governs technical changes such as releases and configurations through change records and approval. Enterprise change management helps people adopt new ways of working through communication, training and reinforcement. An ERP rollout needs both. Letting IT change control lead looks reasonable for a technical project, but benefits are realized only when staff adopt the new processes.

wrong_explanations.A: The disciplines differ in scope and methods: one controls technical change, the other manages people and organizational adoption.
wrong_explanations.C: Controlling releases protects systems, but value depends on users adopting new processes. Treating ERP as purely technical risks failed adoption.
wrong_explanations.D: Organizational change work does not control releases or configurations. Dropping IT change control exposes systems to unauthorized change.

tips: Eliminate: A merges two different disciplines, and D removes control over technical changes.
Final two: B beats C because business value depends on people adopting the change, not only on controlled releases.
Exam cue: when a project changes both systems and how people work, expect an answer that addresses both.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 (Change Enablement); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes); COBIT 2019 BAI05 (Managed Organizational Change); Prosci ADKAR Model
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT change management vs enterprise change management distinction, complements d2_095 (enterprise CM stakeholder management) and d2_104 (failed M&A integration)'. Public source: ITIL 4 + Prosci + Kotter. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Multi-Cloud Governance Under Regulatory Data Sovereignty
questions.question: A SaaS firm runs different cloud providers by region, and a major EU customer demands provable EU data residency. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Move EU customer data to a sovereign EU cloud right away
options.B: Consolidate onto one global provider to simplify governance
options.C: Wait until regulators issue final, binding residency rules
options.D: Enforce residency per region and maintain an exit plan

questions.key_concept: Data-sovereignty pressure is met proportionately: documented, enforced residency per region with transfer safeguards and a ready exit option.
questions.pre_read: Notice the customer wants provable residency, not a new provider. Ask which option proves it without unnecessary disruption.
questions.correct_explanation: The customer needs provable EU residency, which can be met within the current architecture by documenting and enforcing residency per region, using transfer safeguards where data crosses borders, and monitoring regulation. An exit plan keeps a sovereign-cloud move available if it becomes mandatory. Migrating immediately also meets the demand, but it accepts large cost and disruption before the risk requires it.

wrong_explanations.A: An immediate migration may satisfy the customer, but it is a costly, disruptive step taken before analysis shows the current region cannot comply.
wrong_explanations.B: One global provider does not resolve residency and adds concentration risk. It simplifies administration, not compliance.
wrong_explanations.C: The customer demand and contract risk are current. Waiting for regulators ignores an immediate business requirement.

tips: Eliminate: B adds concentration without solving residency, and C ignores a current customer requirement.
Final two: D beats A because a proportionate, risk-based response proves residency now and keeps migration available if needed.
Exam cue: when pressure is real but not yet mandated, prefer the proportionate control plus a contingency over drastic action.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Articles 44-50 (Transfers); EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on Supplementary Measures; CJEU Schrems II Judgment (C-311/18); PIPL (China); DPDPA (India)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Multi-cloud governance under data sovereignty pressure - comprehensive approach, complements d2_087 (multi-cloud governance) and d2_030 (transborder decision)'. questions.subtopic: Strategic Plan vs Unanticipated Major Breach
questions.question: Eight months into a three-year IT strategy, a major breach exposes two million customer records and the CISO requests $25M in unplanned security funding. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Validate the request with a root-cause and residual-risk assessment
options.B: Keep the strategy and handle the breach via incident management
options.C: Defer strategy changes until regulatory inquiries are resolved
options.D: Approve the $25M request now and revisit the strategy later

questions.key_concept: Unplanned post-breach investment must first rest on a root-cause and residual-risk assessment, so funding targets the actual gaps.
questions.pre_read: Notice the funding request comes before anyone knows why the breach happened. Ask what evidence must exist first.
questions.correct_explanation: Before any strategy or budget decision, management needs to know which control failures caused the breach and what risk remains. A root-cause and residual-risk assessment shows whether $25M targets the real gaps and gives the board evidence for reprioritizing. Approving the funds now feels decisive, but it commits capital to an unvalidated request that may miss the causes or crowd out other priorities.

wrong_explanations.B: Incident response fixes the immediate issue, but a breach of this size changes risk and priorities, which the strategy must reflect.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for inquiries to close leaves known weaknesses and customer-trust issues unaddressed for months.
wrong_explanations.D: Approving before assessment commits $25M without evidence that it addresses the breach's causes, and bypasses portfolio governance.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a strategic event as an incident only, and C delays response to known weaknesses.
Final two: A beats D because investment should follow evidence of what failed; funding first may target the wrong gaps.
Exam cue: when a large unplanned spend follows an incident, assess root cause and residual risk before funding.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 APO13 (Managed Security); ISACA Information Security Management Audit/Assurance Program

questions.subtopic: Risk Register Prioritization with Conflicting Executive Views
questions.question: Four executives each push a different set of risks to the top of a bank's register. What should the IS auditor recommend to the CRO as the BEST basis for prioritization?

options.A: Follow the executive with the most organizational influence
options.B: Give equal weight to each executive's preferred risks
options.C: Rank risks by expected loss against board-approved appetite
options.D: Escalate the ranking decision to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: Risk prioritization rests on analysis against board-approved appetite, with regulatory obligations treated as non-discretionary, not on executive preference.
questions.pre_read: Notice each executive has a strong argument. Ask which option gives an objective basis everyone can accept.
questions.correct_explanation: An objective ranking uses expected loss measured against the board-approved risk appetite, treats mandatory regulatory items as non-discretionary, and records any deviation with a rationale. That gives the CRO and the board a defensible basis. Escalating to the audit committee seems appropriate for a deadlock, but the committee oversees; it should receive an analytical ranking to approve, not an unresolved dispute to settle.

wrong_explanations.A: Influence is not a measure of risk. Prioritizing by politics leaves material exposures untreated.
wrong_explanations.B: Equal weighting treats unequal risks as equal and ignores appetite. It produces a compromise, not a risk-based ranking.
wrong_explanations.D: The committee oversees rather than manages. Escalating without analysis passes management's job upward and gives the committee nothing objective to judge.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by politics, and B averages opinions instead of measuring risk.
Final two: C beats D because management must prioritize against appetite; the committee oversees and approves that analysis.
Exam cue: when opinions conflict on risk, choose the option that measures against approved appetite.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk register prioritization under conflicting executive views - analytical method, complements d2_127 (multi-risk treatment trade-offs)'. questions.subtopic: Privacy Program Rollout in M&A Integration
questions.question: Eight weeks before a US–EU health-tech merger closes, the Chief Privacy Officer asks the IS auditor how to combine the HIPAA and GDPR programs. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Meet each regime's rules within one shared governance baseline
options.B: Adopt the stricter GDPR program as the single enterprise standard
options.C: Extend the acquirer's HIPAA program across the acquired EU business
options.D: Run separate programs and defer integration until a year after close

questions.key_concept: When an entity falls under two privacy regimes, it must meet each regime's specific requirements within a shared governance baseline.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether either single framework fully covers the other regime's specific obligations.
questions.correct_explanation: The combined entity must comply with both regimes from Day 1, so the program should meet HIPAA's and GDPR's specific obligations while sharing one data-governance baseline, joint data-flow mapping and clear officer accountability. Adopting GDPR as the single standard is tempting because it is stricter overall, but it does not cover HIPAA-specific duties such as business associate agreements and HIPAA breach-notification rules.

wrong_explanations.B: GDPR is broader, but it does not satisfy HIPAA-specific requirements such as business associate agreements, so US health-data obligations would go unmet.
wrong_explanations.C: HIPAA does not address GDPR duties such as lawful basis, data-subject rights and transfer rules, leaving EU data noncompliant from Day 1.
wrong_explanations.D: Both regimes apply from the day the deal closes. Deferring integration leaves cross-entity data flows ungoverned during the riskiest period.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores GDPR duties for EU data, and D leaves Day-1 data flows ungoverned.
Final two: A beats B because compliance means meeting each regime's specific rules; a stricter framework is not a superset of another.
Exam cue: when two regulatory regimes apply, choose the option that satisfies both, not the one that picks a winner.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR; HIPAA Privacy Rule; HIPAA Security Rule; HIPAA Breach Notification Rule; ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (Privacy Information Management)
