questions.question: A policy requires 'strong authentication' for remote access, but no standard defines it, and three regions implement it differently. Which concern is GREATEST for the IS auditor?

options.A: Without a defined standard, compliance cannot be judged consistently
options.B: Regional control owners may not test their methods regularly
options.C: One region's method may prove weaker than the other two
options.D: Some regions may be spending more on authentication than others

questions.key_concept: Standards make policy measurable; without one, implementations diverge and compliance cannot be assessed consistently.
questions.pre_read: Ask which document should define 'strong', and what happens when it is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy states intent; a standard turns 'strong authentication' into a measurable requirement, such as specific factors. Without one, each region interprets the policy its own way, and neither management nor the auditor can judge compliance consistently. A weaker regional method is a real possibility, but it is a symptom of the missing standard; fixing only that region leaves the root cause and future drift in place.

wrong_explanations.B: Testing needs a defined requirement to test against. Without the standard, owners would only confirm each region's own interpretation.
wrong_explanations.C: A weak regional method is a symptom. The root cause is the missing standard, which lets every region interpret the policy differently.
wrong_explanations.D: Spending differences are not the control issue. The concern is whether authentication meets a defined, measurable requirement.

tips: Eliminate: B tests against a requirement that does not exist, and D shifts the focus to cost.
Final two: A beats C because the missing standard is the root cause; a weak regional method is one symptom of it.
Exam cue: when a policy uses vague terms, look for the standard that makes it measurable; without it, compliance cannot be tested.

questions.subtopic: IT Policy Approval. Senior Management Mandate
questions.question: An IS auditor finds the CISO wrote and approved the enterprise information security policy, and no one else reviewed it. Which concern is GREATEST?

options.A: The policy may contain technical errors that peers would have caught
options.B: The policy may not be mapped to the enterprise's control framework
options.C: The CISO may lack the time to keep the policy current
options.D: The policy lacks top management's mandate and business alignment

questions.key_concept: Policies need top management or board approval for authority and business alignment; approval by a functional head such as the CISO gives neither.
questions.pre_read: Ask what gives a policy its authority across the whole enterprise.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy carries authority only when top management or the board approves it, which signals the mandate, ties it to business objectives and makes it binding enterprise-wide. A CISO is a functional head, not top management, so self-approval lets business units treat the policy as an IT preference. Peer review would catch technical errors, but accuracy is secondary when the policy has no enforceable mandate.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer review helps quality, but technical accuracy is secondary. Without top management approval, even a flawless policy lacks the authority to be enforced.
wrong_explanations.B: Framework mapping aids traceability and can be added at the next review. It does not give the policy the authority to be enforced.
wrong_explanations.C: Workload may affect upkeep, but that is a resourcing issue. The core flaw is that no one with authority endorsed the policy.

tips: Eliminate: B is a mapping point fixable at the next review, and C is a workload issue rather than a governance gap.
Final two: D beats A because a policy without top management approval lacks authority; technical errors matter less.
Exam cue: policies are approved by top management or the board, not by a functional head such as the CISO; standards and procedures can be approved lower down.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the board does not check whether IT use complies with laws and internal policies. Which ISO/IEC 38500:2015 principle is MOST directly unmet?

options.A: Performance
options.B: Continuity
options.C: Conformance
options.D: Confidentiality

questions.key_concept: ISO/IEC 38500:2015 has six principles; Conformance covers compliance with laws and policies. The 2024 edition reframes them under ISO 37000's principles.
questions.pre_read: Recall the six ISO/IEC 38500:2015 principles. Match the gap described, compliance with laws and policies, to one of them.
questions.correct_explanation: ISO/IEC 38500:2015 defines six principles for the governance of IT. Conformance requires that IT use complies with mandatory legislation, regulation and internal policies, which is exactly the oversight the board is missing. Performance is also a 38500 principle and is easy to confuse, but it concerns whether IT is fit for purpose and supports business needs, not legal or policy compliance.

wrong_explanations.A: Performance is a 38500 principle, but it covers IT being fit for purpose and meeting business needs, not compliance.
wrong_explanations.B: Continuity is a business continuity concern, not one of the six ISO/IEC 38500:2015 governance principles.
wrong_explanations.D: Confidentiality is an information security property, not one of the six ISO/IEC 38500:2015 governance principles.

tips: Eliminate: B and D are continuity and security properties, not ISO/IEC 38500:2015 governance principles.
Final two: C beats A because Conformance covers laws and policies, while Performance covers fitness for purpose.
Exam cue: map compliance gaps to Conformance and fitness-for-purpose gaps to Performance in ISO/IEC 38500:2015.

questions.subtopic: IT Strategy Committee vs IT Steering Committee
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the charter of a newly formed IT steering committee. Which responsibility is MOST appropriate to find in it?

options.A: Prioritizing IT projects and allocating resources to them
options.B: Advising the board on emerging technology and long-term IT direction
options.C: Approving routine change requests in daily IT operations
options.D: Providing independent assurance over IT controls

questions.key_concept: The IT steering committee is a management body that prioritizes projects, allocates resources and monitors delivery; the IT strategy committee advises the board.
questions.pre_read: Separate the board-level IT strategy committee from the management-level steering committee. Ask which duty belongs at management level.
questions.correct_explanation: An IT steering committee works at executive management level: it prioritizes projects, allocates resources and monitors delivery against business objectives. Advising the board on emerging technology and long-term direction is a genuine committee role, which makes it tempting, but it belongs to the board-level IT strategy committee, not the steering committee. Mixing the two blurs governance and management responsibilities.

wrong_explanations.B: Advising the board on long-term direction is the role of the board-level IT strategy committee, not the steering committee.
wrong_explanations.C: Routine change approval belongs to operational change management, such as a change advisory board, not a senior committee.
wrong_explanations.D: Independent assurance is internal audit's role. A management committee cannot independently assure its own decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C is routine operational work, and D is internal audit's independent assurance role.
Final two: A beats B because the steering committee manages the portfolio, while advising the board is the strategy committee's job.
Exam cue: strategy committee advises the board; steering committee prioritizes, resources and monitors projects for management.

questions.subtopic: ITIL 4. Four Dimensions of Service Management
questions.question: A service manager reviews culture, roles and staff competencies for a new ITIL 4 service. Which dimension of service management is MOST directly being assessed?

options.A: Value streams and processes
options.B: Organizations and people
options.C: Strategy, design and transition
options.D: Plan, build and run

questions.key_concept: ITIL 4's four dimensions are Organizations and people, Information and technology, Partners and suppliers, and Value streams and processes.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four ITIL 4 dimensions. Match culture, roles and competencies to the dimension about structures and staff.
questions.correct_explanation: ITIL 4 defines four dimensions of service management. Organizations and people covers structures, culture, roles, responsibilities and staff competencies, which is exactly what the manager is reviewing. Value streams and processes is also a real dimension and can mention roles, but it focuses on how activities and workflows create value, not on culture and people capability.

wrong_explanations.A: Value streams and processes is a real dimension, but it covers workflows and activities, not culture and staff competencies.
wrong_explanations.C: Strategy, design and transition are ITIL v3 lifecycle stages, not ITIL 4 dimensions.
wrong_explanations.D: Plan, build and run is a general IT operating model, not one of the ITIL 4 dimensions.

tips: Eliminate: C lists ITIL v3 lifecycle stages, and D is a generic operating model, not an ITIL 4 dimension.
Final two: B beats A because culture, roles and competencies belong to people, while value streams cover workflows.
Exam cue: when a question lists culture, skills or structures, map it to the Organizations and people dimension.

questions.subtopic: Three Lines Model. Roles and Responsibilities
questions.question: The chief risk officer asks internal audit to run the IT risk management process until a new risk manager is hired. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The risk register may lack enough detail on IT risks
options.B: The risk function may lose budget for the vacant post
options.C: Audit staff may lack specialist IT risk skills
options.D: Audit would later be assuring a process it operated

questions.key_concept: Internal audit should not operate second-line risk management; doing so impairs its objectivity when it later provides assurance.
questions.pre_read: Ask which line of the Three Lines Model the task belongs to, and what that means for audit.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the Three Lines Model, internal audit gives independent assurance over risk management, so running the second-line process itself would mean auditing its own work. A skills gap is a real practical risk, but it could be closed through training or support, whereas the loss of objectivity cannot be fixed while audit operates the process.

wrong_explanations.A: Register detail is a quality issue for the risk function to fix, not the main threat.
wrong_explanations.B: Budget for the post is a management matter and does not affect assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Skills can be developed or supplemented; independence lost by operating the process cannot.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are management issues that do not touch audit's role.
Final two: D beats C because operating a process destroys objectivity; skills gaps can be closed.
Exam cue: when audit is asked to perform first- or second-line work, the main concern is independence.

questions.subtopic: KPI vs KRI. Performance and Risk Indicators
questions.question: A vendor-risk KRI has exceeded its threshold for three months; the breaches show on a dashboard but trigger nothing. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Investigate the vendors driving the KRI and report to the CRO
options.B: Link each KRI threshold to an owner and escalation
options.C: Add a second KRI and threshold to confirm the trend
options.D: Report the KRI to the board more often than quarterly

questions.key_concept: KRI thresholds need assigned owners and defined escalation so a breach leads to timely risk response.
questions.pre_read: Notice the KRI works but nothing happens. Ask what is missing between signal and action.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI only reduces risk if a breach triggers a response, so each threshold needs a named owner and a defined escalation and action. Reporting it to the board more often raises visibility, but without an owner obliged to act, the board simply sees the same unaddressed breach more frequently.

wrong_explanations.A: A one-off investigation handles this breach but leaves future breaches with no owner or required response.
wrong_explanations.C: Three months above threshold is already a trend; another indicator delays the response and still assigns no one to act.
wrong_explanations.D: More frequent reporting adds visibility but still assigns no one to act.

tips: Eliminate: A fixes this breach once, and C delays action by measuring a trend that is already clear.
Final two: B beats D because ownership and escalation create action; more reporting only adds visibility.
Exam cue: a KRI threshold is useful only when a breach triggers a defined owner and response.

questions.subtopic: IT Procedures. Ownership and Periodic Review
questions.question: An IS auditor finds operations procedures were written by the staff who run them, have no named owner and were last reviewed four years ago. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have internal audit review and update the procedures each year
options.B: Replace the procedures with the higher-level IT security policy
options.C: Assign an owner for each procedure and require periodic review
options.D: Rewrite the procedures now using a standard corporate template

questions.key_concept: Procedures need named owners and periodic, change-triggered review to stay accurate; one-off rewrites decay.
questions.pre_read: Ask what keeps a document current over time, not just how to fix it today.
questions.correct_explanation: Procedures go stale as systems and roles change, so each needs a named owner accountable for keeping it accurate, a scheduled review and a review after significant change. Rewriting everything now into a standard template fixes today's content, but without ownership and a review cycle the procedures will drift out of date again. Staff writing their own procedures is fine; unowned documents are the problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Maintaining procedures is management's job. Internal audit would end up auditing documents it maintains, which impairs independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Policies state intent, not steps. Staff still need detailed procedures to perform tasks consistently.
wrong_explanations.D: A one-time rewrite improves today's content only. Without an owner and review cycle, the procedures will drift out of date again.

tips: Eliminate: A gives document upkeep to internal audit, and B swaps step-by-step procedures for high-level policy.
Final two: C beats D because ownership and periodic review keep procedures current; a one-off rewrite decays again.
Exam cue: every policy document needs a named owner, a review cycle and change triggers; look for the sustainable fix.

questions.subtopic: IT Policy Management. Document and Version Control
questions.question: Staff at a bank use three versions of the IT acceptable use policy, kept on shared drives and in old emails. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Storage space is wasted by duplicate copies of the policy
options.B: Management may be unable to show which version staff accepted
options.C: Older versions may not show the policy owner or next review date
options.D: Staff may follow superseded rules without knowing it

questions.key_concept: Policy documents need version control and a single authoritative source so staff follow the current rules.
questions.pre_read: Ask what goes wrong in daily operations when nobody knows which version is current.
questions.correct_explanation: Without document control, staff cannot tell which version is current, so they may apply superseded rules and the policy fails at its purpose of directing behavior. A central repository with version control and withdrawal of old copies addresses this. Being unable to show which version staff accepted is a genuine evidence problem, but it matters mainly after an incident; following the wrong rules helps cause one.

wrong_explanations.A: Storage cost is trivial. Duplicate copies matter only because people might follow the wrong one.
wrong_explanations.B: Proof of acceptance is an evidence gap that matters when enforcing after a breach. Staff applying superseded rules is the control failure itself, so it is the greater risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Missing owner and review details are a document-control gap, but they do not change what staff do. The risk lies in staff applying rules that are no longer current.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about storage, and C about missing document details; neither changes how staff behave.
Final two: D beats B because applying outdated rules is the control failure itself; weak proof of acceptance matters later.
Exam cue: for policy documents, look for one controlled current version, with old copies withdrawn and changes communicated.

questions.question: The CIO tells the board IT is efficient because its cost per user is 20% below a published peer benchmark. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important before accepting this claim?

options.A: Whether the benchmark report comes from a well-known, reputable publisher
options.B: Whether IT costs fell compared with the previous year
options.C: Whether peers measure cost and service scope the same way
options.D: Whether the board has approved the use of benchmarks

questions.key_concept: Benchmark comparisons are valid only when cost definitions, scope and service levels are comparable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else, besides efficiency, could make cost per user look low.
questions.correct_explanation: A benchmark supports a conclusion only if the comparison is like for like. If peers include costs this firm excludes, such as end-user support or security, or deliver different service levels, a lower cost per user may reflect a narrower scope or poorer service rather than efficiency. The publisher's reputation matters, but even a reputable benchmark misleads when the cost definitions do not match.

wrong_explanations.A: A reputable source improves credibility, but it cannot fix a comparison where peers count different costs or deliver different services.
wrong_explanations.B: Year-on-year change is a different question. It says nothing about whether the peer comparison is valid.
wrong_explanations.D: Board approval of benchmarking does not make any particular comparison valid. Comparability is what decides the claim.

tips: Eliminate: B answers a different question, and D treats approval as proof of validity.
Final two: C beats A because comparability decides a benchmark's meaning; a reputable publisher cannot fix mismatched scope.
Exam cue: before accepting any benchmark claim, check that definitions, scope and service levels are like for like.

questions.question: QA reviewers at an insurer reject code based on personal judgment because no coding or documentation standards exist, and developers dispute every finding. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Set documented standards for reviews to measure against
options.B: Replace the QA reviewers with more experienced staff
options.C: Have the development manager settle every disputed finding
options.D: Limit QA reviews to the highest-risk releases

questions.key_concept: Quality assurance needs documented standards as review criteria; without them, reviews are subjective and findings disputable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reviewer should measure the code against.
questions.correct_explanation: Quality assurance checks work against agreed requirements, so without documented coding and documentation standards every review is opinion and every finding can be argued. Defining standards first gives developers clear expectations and makes reviews consistent and defensible. More experienced reviewers might judge better, but their findings would still rest on personal judgment, so disputes and inconsistency would continue.

wrong_explanations.B: Experience improves judgment, but reviews would still rest on opinion. Without written standards, findings stay inconsistent and disputable.
wrong_explanations.C: The development manager is not independent of the code. Letting them settle disputes undermines QA and does not fix missing standards.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk-based focus sounds sensible, but it only shrinks scope. Releases still reviewed would be judged without standards, so the disputes continue.

tips: Eliminate: C hands disputes to a conflicted manager, and D cuts QA coverage.
Final two: A beats B because reviews need written criteria; better reviewers still apply only personal judgment.
Exam cue: QA needs defined standards before it can assure anything; look for the criteria first.

questions.subtopic: Quality Management. Root Cause and Continual Improvement
questions.question: The same types of defects recur in every release at a payments firm, and QA logs them but takes no further action. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add more test cases to catch these defects before release
options.B: Report defect counts to the steering committee each month
options.C: Analyze root causes and fix the processes behind them
options.D: Assign an owner to track each logged defect to closure

questions.key_concept: Recurring defects call for root cause analysis and process correction, the continual-improvement core of quality management.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the same defects keep appearing and what would stop them being created.
questions.correct_explanation: Recurring defects show that their causes sit in the process, not in individual releases. Root cause analysis followed by process changes, the corrective-action and continual-improvement step of quality management, stops the defects being created. Adding test cases would catch more of them before release, which helps, but the team would keep producing the same defects and paying to find them each cycle.

wrong_explanations.A: More test cases catch defects but do not stop them being created. The cost of finding the same defects recurs every release.
wrong_explanations.B: Monthly reporting adds visibility but no action. The committee would simply watch the same defects recur.
wrong_explanations.D: Tracking each defect to closure fixes individual defects, but nothing analyzes why the same types keep appearing.

tips: Eliminate: B only reports the problem, and D closes defects one by one without asking why they recur.
Final two: C beats A because removing causes prevents recurrence; more tests only catch the same defects again.
Exam cue: recurring problems call for root cause analysis and corrective action, the core of continual improvement.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds an IT quality program checks only that releases match technical specifications, yet many releases fail acceptance by the departments that requested them. Which weakness is GREATEST?

options.A: The technical specifications may lack enough detail to test against
options.B: Users may be too critical when they test new releases
options.C: The QA team may be testing too few releases each quarter
options.D: Quality criteria are not tied to business and user requirements

questions.key_concept: Quality criteria must trace to business and user requirements; technical conformance alone does not prove fitness for purpose.
questions.pre_read: Ask who defines quality, and whether the QA checks reflect that definition.
questions.correct_explanation: Quality means fitness for purpose as defined by the customer, so quality criteria must trace to business and user requirements. A program that checks only technical conformance can pass releases that meet the specification yet fail the business. More detailed specifications would sharpen technical testing, but if the specifications do not reflect user needs, greater detail only confirms the wrong thing more precisely.

wrong_explanations.A: More detail sharpens conformance testing, but if specifications miss user needs, releases still pass QA and fail the business.
wrong_explanations.B: Blaming users ignores the pattern. Consistent rejections show the quality criteria miss what users need.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing more releases against the same criteria would just pass more releases that users reject. Coverage is not the gap.

tips: Eliminate: B blames the users, and C adds coverage with the same flawed criteria.
Final two: D beats A because quality must trace to user needs; more detailed specifications can still miss them.
Exam cue: quality is fitness for purpose; if requesters reject what QA passes, check where the quality criteria come from.
